questions.stem: A patient is brought to the emergency after a fall from a tree. He developed shortness of breath and chest pain, is tachypneic, and has distended neck veins on examination. His chest X-ray shows as follows: Which of the following is the correct finding here?
questions.stemHtml: A patient is brought to the emergency after a fall from a tree. He developed shortness of breath and chest pain, is tachypneic, and has distended neck veins on examination. His chest X-ray shows as follows: Which of the following is the correct finding here?
questions.solution: Correct Answer: C) Collapsed lung The above clinical symptoms and the chest X-ray lead to the diagnosis of a right pneumothorax, which causes the lung to collapse and squished towards the hilum, ipsilateral depression of the hemidiaphragm, and contralateral deviation of the mediastinum. Pathophysiology: The pressure gradient in the thorax changes with pneumothorax. Normally, the pleural space is negative compared to atmospheric pressure. If air enters the pleural space through communication with the alveoli, it alters the pressure gradient, leading to lung collapse. Radiographic appearance of pneumothorax: Pneumothorax appears as a radiolucent area (black). Pneumothorax pushes the adjacent lung towards the hilum. A sharp radiopaque line separates the pneumothorax from the lung parenchyma. A closed pneumothorax is easily detectable in an expiratory X-ray, as there is a decrease in lung volume. However, the volume of the pneumothorax is not affected by respiration. Tension Pneumothorax Significant contralateral deviation of the mediastinum (vs Option A) Collapsed lung Depression of ipsilateral hemidiaphragm (vs Option B) contralateral tension pneumothorax during pneumonectomy.” Anesthesia and analgesia 106 1 (2008): 58-60, table of contents ." data-hash="8932" data-license="OPEN ACCESS" data-source="https://journals.lww.com/anesthesia-analgesia/fulltext/2008/01000/intraoperative_contralateral_tension_pneumothorax.9.aspx" data-tags="April2025" height="382" src="https://image.prepladder.com/notes/GNIKM49bS7b80ApD8HsL1744317108.png" width="400" /> {{caption_text}} White-out lung (Option D) refers to when there is complete opacification of an entire hemithorax. questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer: C) Collapsed lung

The above clinical symptoms and the chest X-ray lead to the diagnosis of a right pneumothorax, which causes the lung to collapse and squished towards the hilum, ipsilateral depression of the hemidiaphragm, and contralateral deviation of the mediastinum.

 

Pathophysiology:

  • The pressure gradient in the thorax changes with pneumothorax. Normally, the pleural space is negative compared to atmospheric pressure.
  • If air enters the pleural space through communication with the alveoli, it alters the pressure gradient, leading to lung collapse.

 

Radiographic appearance of pneumothorax:

  • Pneumothorax appears as a radiolucent area (black).
  • Pneumothorax pushes the adjacent lung towards the hilum.
  • A sharp radiopaque line separates the pneumothorax from the lung parenchyma.
  • A closed pneumothorax is easily detectable in an expiratory X-ray, as there is a decrease in lung volume. However, the volume of the pneumothorax is not affected by respiration.

Tension Pneumothorax

  • Significant contralateral deviation of the mediastinum (vs Option A)
  • Collapsed lung
  • Depression of ipsilateral hemidiaphragm (vs Option B)

White-out lung (Option D) refers to when there is complete opacification of an entire hemithorax. This is seen in conditions like pneumonia of the entire lung, a large mass in the lung or chest wall, large pleural effusion, etc., which increase the opacity of the lung.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old patient is recovering from pneumonia and has been on mechanical ventilation for the past week. The medical team is preparing to assess the patient for readiness to wean off the ventilator. Which of the following criteria should the medical team confirm before initiating the weaning process?
questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old patient is recovering from pneumonia and has been on mechanical ventilation for the past week. The medical team is preparing to assess the patient for readiness to wean off the ventilator. Which of the following criteria should the medical team confirm before initiating the weaning process?
questions.solution: ; 5 mL/kg Explanation: A tidal volume greater than 5 mL/kg supports the decision to initiate weaning, indicating adequate respiratory function. Discontinuing mechanical ventilation involves two phases: Readiness testing and Weaning. Readiness Testing: Assess if the underlying cause for ventilation is controlled or reversed. Manage complicating factors such as bronchospasm, heart failure, infection, malnutrition, increased CO₂ production, acid-base imbalances, anemia, altered mental status, and sleep deprivation. Weaning is considered when the patient meets the following criteria: pH > 7.25, Adequate oxygenation (FiO₂ < 0.5, PaO₂ saturation > 90%), Hemodynamic stability, and no signs of myocardial ischemia. Adequate cough reflex present. Weaning or Liberation: Key measurements for weaning criteria: Inspiratory pressure : < –25 cm H₂O Tidal volume (VT) : > 5 mL/kg Vital capacity : > 10 mL/kg (Option A) Minute ventilation : < 10 L/min (Option B) Rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI) : < 100 (with < 105 indicating potential for extubation). (Option D) Weaning methods: SIMV : Gradually decrease mechanical breaths and pressure support to 5–8 cm H₂O while maintaining acceptable arterial CO₂ tension and respiratory rate. PSV : Gradually reduce pressure support to maintain a VT of 4–6 mL/kg and respiratory rate < 30. T-Piece/CPAP : Observe spontaneous breathing; use sequential trials if needed. CPAP (5 cm H₂O) may prevent atelectasis during prolonged T-piece trials by maintaining functional residual capacity (FRC). @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
; 5 mL/kg

Explanation:

A tidal volume greater than 5 mL/kg supports the decision to initiate weaning, indicating adequate respiratory function.

Discontinuing mechanical ventilation involves two phases: Readiness testing and Weaning.

  • Readiness Testing:
    • Assess if the underlying cause for ventilation is controlled or reversed.
    • Manage complicating factors such as bronchospasm, heart failure, infection, malnutrition, increased CO₂ production, acid-base imbalances, anemia, altered mental status, and sleep deprivation.
    • Weaning is considered when the patient meets the following criteria:
      • pH > 7.25,
      • Adequate oxygenation (FiO₂ < 0.5, PaO₂ saturation > 90%),
      • Hemodynamic stability, and no signs of myocardial ischemia.
      • Adequate cough reflex present.
  • Weaning or Liberation:
    • Key measurements for weaning criteria:
      • Inspiratory pressure: < –25 cm H₂O
      • Tidal volume (VT): > 5 mL/kg
      • Vital capacity: > 10 mL/kg (Option A)
      • Minute ventilation: < 10 L/min (Option B)
      • Rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI): < 100 (with < 105 indicating potential for extubation). (Option D)
    • Weaning methods:
      • SIMV: Gradually decrease mechanical breaths and pressure support to 5–8 cm H₂O while maintaining acceptable arterial CO₂ tension and respiratory rate.
      • PSV: Gradually reduce pressure support to maintain a VT of 4–6 mL/kg and respiratory rate < 30.
      • T-Piece/CPAP: Observe spontaneous breathing; use sequential trials if needed. CPAP (5 cm H₂O) may prevent atelectasis during prolonged T-piece trials by maintaining functional residual capacity (FRC).

questions.stem: A 7 Y/O boy presents with a limp and complains of pain in his right hip that has gradually worsened over the past few weeks. The pain is sometimes referred to his knee.There is no history of trauma.On physical examination, there is a limited range of motion, particularly in internal rotation and abduction of the hip.X-ray of the pelvis shows flattening of the femoral head with areas of sclerosis and fragmentation.What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 7 Y/O boy presents with a limp and complains of pain in his right hip that has gradually worsened over the past few weeks. The pain is sometimes referred to his knee.There is no history of trauma.On physical examination, there is a limited range of motion, particularly in internal rotation and abduction of the hip.X-ray of the pelvis shows flattening of the femoral head with areas of sclerosis and fragmentation.What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: ong>, is an idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head that typically affects children between the ages of 4 and 10. Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease Description Idiopathic osteonecrosis or idiopathic avascular necrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis of the femoral head. Etiopathogenesis Idiopathic or etiology that would disrupt the blood flow to femoral epiphysis. Coagulopathy and steroid use. Includes 4 phases Necrosis : Disruption of the blood supply leads to infarction of the femoral capital epiphysis. Fragmentation : The body reabsorbs the infarcted bone. Reossification : Osteoblastic activity takes over, and the femoral epiphysis reestablishes. Remodeling : The new femoral head may be enlarged or flattened. It reshapes during growth. Risk factors Ten percent familial (there is a delayed bone age by about 2 years) HIV (Up to 5% of HIV patients have avascular necrosis of the hip) Factor V Leiden Thrombophilias (increased clotting) Hypofibrinolysis (decreased ability to dissolve clots) Secondhand smoke exposure Low socioeconomic status Birth weight less than 2.5 kg in boys Short stature Clinical features Limp of acute or insidious onset, usually painless. If pain is present, it is localized to the hip or knee. Decreased internal rotation and abduction of hip. Atrophy of thighs and buttocks. Leg length discrepancy. Antalgic gait in acute cases Trendelenburg gait in chronic cases Diagnosis Standard anteroposterior pelvis and frog-leg lateral (Lauenstein) views. Bone scan or MRI Early findings: Widening of joint space (epiphyseal cartilage hypertrophy) Changes in the epiphysis. Crescent sign: Subchondral radiolucent zone of the anterolateral epiphysis Late signs: Flattening of the femoral head. Bone scan shows decreased perfusion to the femoral head. questions.solutionHtml:
ong>, is an idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head that typically affects children between the ages of 4 and 10.

 

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease

Description
  • Idiopathic osteonecrosis or idiopathic avascular necrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis of the femoral head.

Etiopathogenesis
  • Idiopathic or etiology that would disrupt the blood flow to femoral epiphysis.
  • Coagulopathy and steroid use.
 

Includes 4 phases

  • Necrosis: Disruption of the blood supply leads to infarction of the femoral capital epiphysis.
  • Fragmentation: The body reabsorbs the infarcted bone.
  • Reossification: Osteoblastic activity takes over, and the femoral epiphysis reestablishes.
  • Remodeling: The new femoral head may be enlarged or flattened. It reshapes during growth.

Risk factors
  • Ten percent familial (there is a delayed bone age by about 2 years)
  • HIV (Up to 5% of HIV patients have avascular necrosis of the hip)
  • Factor V Leiden
  • Thrombophilias (increased clotting)
  • Hypofibrinolysis (decreased ability to dissolve clots)
  • Secondhand smoke exposure
  • Low socioeconomic status
  • Birth weight less than 2.5 kg in boys
  • Short stature

Clinical features
  • Limp of acute or insidious onset, usually painless.
  • If pain is present, it is localized to the hip or knee.
  • Decreased internal rotation and abduction of hip.
  • Atrophy of thighs and buttocks.
  • Leg length discrepancy.
  • Antalgic gait in acute cases
  • Trendelenburg gait in chronic cases

Diagnosis
  • Standard anteroposterior pelvis and frog-leg lateral (Lauenstein) views.
  • Bone scan or MRI


 

Early findings:

  • Widening of joint space (epiphyseal cartilage hypertrophy)
  • Changes in the epiphysis.
  • Crescent sign: Subchondral radiolucent zone of the anterolateral epiphysis
 

Late signs:

  • Flattening of the femoral head.
  • Bone scan shows decreased perfusion to the femoral head.

Differential diagnosis
  • Transient synovitis
  • Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED)
  • Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia (SED)
  • Gaucher disease
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Meyer dysplasia

Treatment

Non operative:

  • Indicated for children with bone age less than 6 or lateral pillar A involvement.
  • Activity restriction and protective weight-bearing are recommended until ossification is complete.
 

Operative treatment:

  • Femoral or Pelvic Osteotomy indicated in children older than 8 years.
  • Valgus or Shelf Osteotomies indicated in children with hinge abduction
  • Hip Arthroscopy

Complications
  • Coxa magna: Widening of the femoral head.
  • Coda plans: Flattening of the femoral head.

 

Gaucher disease (Option B): A lysosomal storage disorder that may affect the bones but usually presents with hepatosplenomegaly and other systemic signs.

Meyer's dysplasia (Option C): A benign condition that affects the growing hip joint, but it typically does not present with hip pain or limp like Perthes disease.

Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (Option D): A hereditary disorder affecting multiple joints, causing pain and early-onset arthritis, but is usually more widespread and affects more than just one hip.

Blood tests reveal a significantly elevated serum calcium level. The patient is diagnosed with hypercalcemia of malignancy. Which of the following is the drug of choice for treating this condition?
questions.solution: "customMeta" data-dictid="5d3892bd481692777183797a2e7318">bisphosphonate that is considered the drug of choice for the treatment of hypercalcemia of malignancy due to its potent ability to inhibit bone resorption and lower serum calcium levels effectively. Management of hypercalcemia in malignancy: Initial Treatment Intravenous hydration with normal saline to increase renal calcium excretion and glomerular filtration rate. Loop diuretics (e.g. furosemide) after initial volume expansion to enhance calciuresis. Pharmacologic Therapy Calcitonin: Provides a rapid but short-lived reduction in serum calcium levels. Bisphosphonates (e.g. Zoledronic acid, Pamidronate) : Potent inhibitors of osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, providing a more sustained reduction in calcium levels. Denosumab: A monoclonal antibody that inhibits osteoclast activity, effective in bisphosphonate-refractory hypercalcemia. Glucocorticoids: Used in calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia to inhibit vitamin D conversion. Refractory Hypercalcemia Denosumab can be used as an alternative for refractory or recurrent hypercalcemia despite treatment with bisphosphonates. "customMeta" data-dictid="5d3892bd481692777183797a2e7318">bisphosphonate that is considered the drug of choice for the treatment of hypercalcemia of malignancy due to its potent ability to inhibit bone resorption and lower serum calcium levels effectively.

Management of hypercalcemia in malignancy:

Initial Treatment

  • Intravenous hydration with normal saline to increase renal calcium excretion and glomerular filtration rate.
  • Loop diuretics (e.g. furosemide) after initial volume expansion to enhance calciuresis.

Pharmacologic Therapy

  • Calcitonin: Provides a rapid but short-lived reduction in serum calcium levels.
  • Bisphosphonates (e.g. Zoledronic acid, Pamidronate): Potent inhibitors of osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, providing a more sustained reduction in calcium levels.
  • Denosumab: A monoclonal antibody that inhibits osteoclast activity, effective in bisphosphonate-refractory hypercalcemia.
  • Glucocorticoids: Used in calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia to inhibit vitamin D conversion.

Refractory Hypercalcemia

  • Denosumab can be used as an alternative for refractory or recurrent hypercalcemia despite treatment with bisphosphonates.
  • Hemodialysis may be considered in patients with advanced kidney disease.

Acute Humoral Rejection (AHR):

  • Definition
    • Significant complication in organ transplantation, particularly in kidney transplants.
    • Characterized by donor-specific antibodies (DSAs) targeting the vascular endothelium, leading to tissue injury and graft dysfunction - Acute process (Option A & C ruled out)
  • Mechanisms of AHR:
    • Binding of DSAs to donor HLA molecules activates the complement system, resulting in:
      • Capillary Injury: Damage to peritubular capillaries is a hallmark of AHR.
      • C4d Deposition: A key diagnostic marker; approximately 30% of acute rejection biopsies show widespread C4d staining.
      • Histological Features: May include neutrophilic infiltration, glomerulitis, and fibrinoid necrosis in severe cases.
  • Diagnostic Criteria
    • Combination of clinical presentation, serological testing, and histopathological findings:
      • Histologic Evidence: Glomerulitis or peritubular capillaritis.
      • Antibody Interaction: Linear C4d staining indicates recent antibody interaction with vascular endothelium.
      • Detection of DSAs: Presence of DSAs in serum confirms diagnosis.
  • Symptoms
    • Acute Elevation in Creatinine: Noted within days to weeks post-transplant.
    • Fever and Malaise
    • Graft Tenderness
  • Treatment: (Option D ruled out)
    • Plasmapheresis: Removes circulating antibodies.
    • Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG): Modulates immune responses.
    • Rituximab: Targets CD20 on B cells to reduce antibody production.
    • Eculizumab: A complement inhibitor effective in severe AHR cases.

Which technique is the scientist most likely using?
questions.solution: RFLP involves DNA digestion with restriction enzymes, gel electrophoresis, transfer to a nitrocellulose membrane, hybridization with labeled probes, and visualization of fragments. Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism (RFLP) Variation in DNA fragment lengths due to differences in DNA sequences when digested with restriction enzymes are used as genetic markers. Applications: Parenthood Disputes, Population Genetics, Genetic Disease Diagnosis, Genetic Mapping, Cloning, Forensic Medicine. Sequential Steps involved using RFLP technique 1. DNA Digestion DNA is cut by restriction enzymes at specific sites. 2. Electrophoresis DNA fragments are separated by size using gel electrophoresis. 3. Denaturation To enable probe binding, the separated fragments are denatured 4. Southern Blotting Fragments are transferred from the gel to a nitrocellulose membrane. 5. Hybridization DNA fragments hybridize with labeled DNA probes. 6. Visualization Hybridized fragments are visualized to reveal the presence or absence of restriction sites. Option B: PCR is used to amplify DNA, not to analyze fragment length variations. Option C: SSCP is used to detect variations in single-stranded DNA based on their conformational differences, not the length of restriction fragments. Option D: DNA sequencing determines the nucleotide order, not the length variation of fragments after restriction enzyme digestion. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
RFLP involves DNA digestion with restriction enzymes, gel electrophoresis, transfer to a nitrocellulose membrane, hybridization with labeled probes, and visualization of fragments.

 

Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism (RFLP)

  • Variation in DNA fragment lengths due to differences in DNA sequences when digested with restriction enzymes are used as genetic markers.
  • Applications: Parenthood Disputes, Population Genetics, Genetic Disease Diagnosis, Genetic Mapping, Cloning, Forensic Medicine.

 

 

                          Sequential Steps involved using RFLP technique 
 

1. DNA Digestion

DNA is cut by restriction enzymes at specific sites.
 

2. Electrophoresis

DNA fragments are separated by size using gel electrophoresis.
 

3. Denaturation

To enable probe binding, the separated fragments are denatured
 

4. Southern Blotting

Fragments are transferred from the gel to a nitrocellulose membrane.
 

5. Hybridization

DNA fragments hybridize with labeled DNA probes.
 

6. Visualization

Hybridized fragments are visualized to reveal the presence or absence of restriction sites.


 

Option B: PCR is used to amplify DNA, not to analyze fragment length variations.

Option C: SSCP is used to detect variations in single-stranded DNA based on their conformational differences, not the length of restriction fragments.

Option D: DNA sequencing determines the nucleotide order, not the length variation of fragments after restriction enzyme digestion.

Steps

Salient points

1

Verification of diagnosis

  • Most important step
  • Examination of a sample of cases and verify the diagnosis
  • To avoid a spurious diagnosis based on signs and symptoms.

2

Confirmation of the existence of an epidemic

  • Compare data collected with the previous year's data.

3

Defining the population at risk

  • Obtain a map of the area affected.

Data analysis

Formulation of hypothesis

Testing of hypothesis

Evaluation of ecological factors

  • Effect of humidity.
  • Effect of sanitary conditions.

9

Further investigation of the population at risk

  • Keep looking for any other population that is at risk.

10

Writing the report

  • To provide a strategy at the end.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic renal failure and resistant oedema was treated with a drug that alleviated the oedema. However, increasing doses were needed over time. Although the drug remained effective, the patient developed involuntary hand twitching and perioral numbness. Which class of drug was given?
questions.stemHtml: A patient with chronic renal failure and resistant oedema was treated with a drug that alleviated the oedema. However, increasing doses were needed over time. Although the drug remained effective, the patient developed involuntary hand twitching and perioral numbness. Which class of drug was given?
questions.solution: Involuntary hand twitching, along with perioral numbness, is suggestive of tetany due to hypocalcemia caused by loop diuretics.. High ceiling diuretics (loop diuretics), which are preferred in treating oedema (including resistant oedema and for rapid fluid mobilisation), impair the absorption of calcium ions, thus causing tetany. Loop diuretics like furosemide primarily inhibit the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, disrupting the reabsorption of sodium, chloride, and water, which normally generates a positive potential gradient in the tubule's lumen. This abolishes the lumen-positive potential, reducing Ca²⁺ reabsorption and causing hypocalcemia . Common Adverse Effects of loop diuretics (also seen with Thiazides, except for Calcium) : Hyponatremia → Hypotension Hypokalemia → Muscle weakness increases the risk of digoxin toxicity Hypocalcemia → Tetany (Thiazides usually increase calcium levels) Hypomagnesemia → Pseudogout Decrease in H+ ions → Metabolic alkalosis Hyperuricemia → in high doses Hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia Ototoxicity Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors(Option B): Weak diuretics, hence are not used in the treatment of edema. Thiazide Diuretics(Option C): They produce hypercalcemia by preserving calcium. Osmotic Diuretics(Option D): Contraindicated in renal failure. @Neet_pg_bot

Involuntary hand twitching, along with perioral numbness, is suggestive of tetany due to hypocalcemia caused by loop diuretics.. High ceiling diuretics (loop diuretics), which are preferred in treating oedema (including resistant oedema and for rapid fluid mobilisation), impair the absorption of calcium ions, thus causing tetany.
  • Loop diuretics like furosemide primarily inhibit the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, disrupting the reabsorption of sodium, chloride, and water, which normally generates a positive potential gradient in the tubule's lumen.

  • This abolishes the lumen-positive potential, reducing Ca²⁺ reabsorption and causing hypocalcemia.

Common Adverse Effects of loop diuretics (also seen with Thiazides, except for Calcium):

  • Hyponatremia → Hypotension
  • Hypokalemia → Muscle weakness increases the risk of digoxin toxicity
  • Hypocalcemia → Tetany (Thiazides usually increase calcium levels)
  • Hypomagnesemia → Pseudogout
  • Decrease in H+ ions → Metabolic alkalosis
  • Hyperuricemia → in high doses
  • Hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia
  • Ototoxicity

Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors(Option B): Weak diuretics, hence are not used in the treatment of edema.   

Thiazide Diuretics(Option C): They produce hypercalcemia by preserving calcium.  
Osmotic Diuretics(Option D): Contraindicated in renal failure.

A

Arcuate Artery
  • Supplies the myometrium(outer ⅓) and gives Radial artery

R

Radial Artery
  • Supplies the myometrium ( inner ⅔)

B

questions.solution: yle="border-collapse:collapse; width:623px"> Levels of Prevention Description Measures Primary Prevention Interventions before the onset of the disease to avert its occurrence by addressing the pre-pathogenesis phase. Promotes facial cleanliness and sanitation to prevent trachoma. Secondary Prevention Aim to halt disease progression in its early stages and prevent complications through timely diagnosis (e.g., screening, case-finding) and prompt, appropriate treatment. Conduct regular eye screenings to detect and treat trachoma early. Tertiary Prevention Focuses on minimizing the impact of existing health conditions by reducing impairments and disabilities , alleviating suffering, and promoting adjustment to irreversible states. Coordinates surgical treatment for those with trachoma-related blindness. Levels of Prevention

Description

Measures

Primary Prevention

Interventions before the onset of the disease to avert its occurrence by addressing the pre-pathogenesis phase.

Promotes facial cleanliness and sanitation to prevent trachoma.

Secondary Prevention

Aim to halt disease progression in its early stages and prevent complications through timely diagnosis (e.g., screening, case-finding) and prompt, appropriate treatment.

Conduct regular eye screenings to detect and treat trachoma early.

Tertiary Prevention

Focuses on minimizing the impact of existing health conditions by reducing impairments and disabilities, alleviating suffering, and promoting adjustment to irreversible states.

Coordinates surgical treatment for those with trachoma-related blindness.

Quaternary Prevention

Promoting evidence-based practices to prevent over diagnosis and offering ethically validated treatment options

Ensures antibiotics are prescribed only to confirmed cases to avoid unnecessary treatment.

This fungus produces green, granular colonies with a distinctive red pigment that diffuses into the agar when cultured on Sabouraud agar, which is a characteristic feature of this organism. Explanation:

Given the patient's symptoms, history of exposure to bamboo rats, and immunocompromised status due to AIDS, microscopy showing septate hyphae with branched conidiophores, the likely pathogen is Talaromyces marneffei. This fungus produces green, granular colonies with a distinctive red pigment that diffuses into the agar when cultured on Sabouraud agar, which is a characteristic feature of this organism.

Diagnosis

Culture on Sabouraud Agar:

  • Green, granular colonies with a distinctive red pigment that diffuses into the agar.

Microscopy:

  • Septate hyphae with branched conidiophores

showing a brush-like arrangement of spores

 

Additional Tests:

  • Antigen testing (urine/serum) and PCR

 

White, cottony, mycelial growth (Option A): It is typically associated with Histoplasma capsulatum. This option is incorrect.

 

Smooth, mucoid, cream-coloured colonies (Option C): It is typically associated with Cryptococcus neoformans. This option is incorrect.

 

Creamy white, smooth colonies and with a yeasty odour (Option D): It is typically associated with Candida albicans. This option is incorrect.

questions.solution: > The above images illustrate the different types of craniosynostosis. Craniosynostosis occurs when one or more skull sutures close prematurely, potentially leading to varying impacts on a child's neurodevelopment depending on the number of sutures affected and the severity of complications. Posterior fontanelle: This smaller fontanelle at the back of the head usually closes within 2 months of birth. Anterior fontanelle: This larger fontanelle at the top of the head usually closes between 7 and 18 months. Scaphocephaly or dolichocephaly (premature fusion of the sagittal suture): These patients have a long, narrow-shaped head with a higher anteroposterior diameter. Anterior plagiocephaly (premature fusion of 1 coronal suture): The forehead appears flat on the affected side, Harlequin sign (high supraorbital margins seen in radiographs), frontal bossing on the unaffected side, and nasal deviation towards the normal side. Posterior plagiocephaly (premature fusion of 1 lambdoid suture): Frontal and occipital bossing, ipsilateral ear moved downward, from above the head looks like a trapeze. Trigonocephaly (premature fusion of the metopic suture): The forehead is narrow and pointed; the head has a triangular shape viewed from above, hypotelorism. Brachycephaly (bi-coronal premature fusion): Short skull, forehead, and occiput flattened but the frontal bone is long (vertically) and prominent, hypertelorism, and Harlequin malformation. @Neet_pg_bot

>
  • The above images illustrate the different types of craniosynostosis.
  • Craniosynostosis occurs when one or more skull sutures close prematurely, potentially leading to varying impacts on a child's neurodevelopment depending on the number of sutures affected and the severity of complications.

Posterior fontanelle: This smaller fontanelle at the back of the head usually closes within 2 months of birth.

Anterior fontanelle: This larger fontanelle at the top of the head usually closes between 7 and 18 months.

Scaphocephaly or dolichocephaly (premature fusion of the sagittal suture):

  • These patients have a long, narrow-shaped head with a higher anteroposterior diameter.

 

Anterior plagiocephaly (premature fusion of 1 coronal suture):

  • The forehead appears flat on the affected side, Harlequin sign (high supraorbital margins seen in radiographs), frontal bossing on the unaffected side, and nasal deviation towards the normal side.

 

Posterior plagiocephaly (premature fusion of 1 lambdoid suture):

  • Frontal and occipital bossing, ipsilateral ear moved downward, from above the head looks like a trapeze.

 

Trigonocephaly (premature fusion of the metopic suture):

  • The forehead is narrow and pointed; the head has a triangular shape viewed from above, hypotelorism.

 

Brachycephaly (bi-coronal premature fusion):

  • Short skull, forehead, and occiput flattened but the frontal bone is long (vertically) and prominent, hypertelorism, and Harlequin malformation.

questions.stem: A patient has a urine concentration of a substance of 10 mg/mL, a urine flow rate of 2 mL/min, and a plasma concentration of that substance of 5 mg/mL. What is the clearance rate of this substance?
questions.stemHtml: A patient has a urine concentration of a substance of 10 mg/mL, a urine flow rate of 2 mL/min, and a plasma concentration of that substance of 5 mg/mL. What is the clearance rate of this substance?
questions.solution: e of plasma completely cleared of a substance by the kidneys per minute (mL/min), reflecting renal excretory efficiency. It is essential for evaluating kidney function, including filtration, reabsorption, and secretion processes. To calculate the clearance rate (Cs) of the substance, use the formula: Clearance Formula : ( Cs) = (Us x V) / Ps Us : Urine concentration of the substance V : Urine flow rate Ps : Plasma concentration of the substance Plugging in the values: Cs = (10 ×2)/5 = 4 ml /min So, the clearance rate of the substance is 4 mL/min . Types of Clearance Measurements: Inulin Clearance Used to measure Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) as it is freely filtered but not reabsorbed or secreted. Not ideal for routine use due to intravenous administration. Creatinine Clearance Estimates GFR using creatinine, which is primarily filtered by the glomeruli. Slightly inaccurate due to tubular secretion, but practical for clinical settings. PAH Clearance Estimates Renal Plasma Flow (RPF). PAH is cleared through both glomerular filtration and tubular secretion. Correction for PAH extraction ratio improves accuracy. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
e of plasma completely cleared of a substance by the kidneys per minute (mL/min), reflecting renal excretory efficiency. It is essential for evaluating kidney function, including filtration, reabsorption, and secretion processes.

 

To calculate the clearance rate (Cs) of the substance, use the formula:

Clearance Formula: (Cs) = (Us x V) / Ps

Us: Urine concentration of the substance

V: Urine flow rate

Ps: Plasma concentration of the substance

Plugging in the values:

Cs = (10 ×2)/5  = 4 ml /min

So, the clearance rate of the substance is 4 mL/min.

Types of Clearance Measurements:

 

Inulin Clearance
  • Used to measure Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) as it is freely filtered but not reabsorbed or secreted.
  • Not ideal for routine use due to intravenous administration.

Creatinine Clearance
  • Estimates GFR using creatinine, which is primarily filtered by the glomeruli.
  • Slightly inaccurate due to tubular secretion, but practical for clinical settings.

PAH Clearance
  • Estimates Renal Plasma Flow (RPF).
  • PAH is cleared through both glomerular filtration and tubular secretion.
  • Correction for PAH extraction ratio improves accuracy.

questions.stem: A patient is asked to hold a piece of paper between their thumb and index finger. When the examiner attempts to pull the paper away, the patient tries to hold the paper as shown in the image. Based on this observation, which muscle is likely affected?
questions.stemHtml: A patient is asked to hold a piece of paper between their thumb and index finger. When the examiner attempts to pull the paper away, the patient tries to hold the paper as shown in the image. Based on this observation, which muscle is likely affected?
questions.solution: strong> Explanation: In this scenario, the patient flexes the distal phalanx of the thumb to grip the paper when the examiner attempts to pull it away, indicating weakness in the adductor pollicis muscle, which is innervated by the ulnar nerve , thereby confirming a positive Froment's test. Froment’s test: Tests Adductor pollicis supplied by Ulnar nerve. The patient is asked to hold a piece of paper (or a card) between the thumb and index finger of the affected hand & card is pulled out. Positive Result: If the patient flexes the distal phalanx of the thumb while attempting to hold the paper, it indicates weakness of the adductor pollicis muscle due to ulnar nerve dysfunction. This flexion occurs due to flexor pollicis longus innervated by the median nerve. Flexor pollicis brevis (Option A) primarily flexes the thumb without significantly contributing to grip strength. Abductor pollicis brevis (Option B) aids in thumb abduction. Opponents pollicis (Option D) facilitates thumb opposition. @Neet_pg_bot

Which among the following surgical procedures can help increase the bowel length and potentially reduce the dependency on parenteral nutrition?
questions.stemHtml: A 6-year-old child with a history of extensive small bowel resection due to necrotizing enterocolitis is diagnosed with short bowel syndrome. Which among the following surgical procedures can help increase the bowel length and potentially reduce the dependency on parenteral nutrition?
questions.solution: trong> The Bianchi procedure/ Longitudinal intestinal lengthening and tailoring (LILT) is recognised as an effective surgical treatment for short bowel syndrome (SBS). Bianchi initially described the procedure for intestinal lengthening where the mesenteric vascular bed is divided into two systems. The enlarged small intestine is split into two parallel segments, each with its own blood supply, and then reconnected. This technique reduces the small intestine's diameter by 50% and doubles its length . Whipple Procedure ( Pancreaticoduodenectomy), Billroth I and II procedures and Ileostomy (Option B, C and D) don't involve intestinal lengthening @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>
  • The Bianchi procedure/ Longitudinal intestinal lengthening and tailoring (LILT) is recognised as an effective surgical treatment for short bowel syndrome (SBS).
  • Bianchi initially described the procedure for intestinal lengthening where the mesenteric vascular bed is divided into two systems.
  • The enlarged small intestine is split into two parallel segments, each with its own blood supply, and then reconnected.
  • This technique reduces the small intestine's diameter by 50% and doubles its length.

 

Whipple Procedure ( Pancreaticoduodenectomy), Billroth I and II procedures and Ileostomy (Option B, C and D) don't involve intestinal lengthening

questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman with a history of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is evaluated at a fertility clinic due to difficulty conceiving. A transvaginal ultrasound shows a follicle with a large fluid-filled antrum and a well-defined cumulus oophorus. Which stage of follicle maturation does this represent?
questions.solution: mMeta" data-dictid="b0c3f6b8901692777203d0446fe1f4">follicle (Mature Follicle) is the final stage before ovulation. It is characterised by a large fluid-filled antrum and a well-defined cumulus oophorus surrounding the oocyte. This stage indicates that the follicle is fully mature and ready to release the oocyte during ovulation. Primordial Follicle (Option C): The initial stage where follicles are in a dormant state . These consist of a primary oocyte surrounded by a single layer of squamous granulosa cells. Primary Follicle (Option A): The primordial follicle matures into a primary follicle where the granulosa cells become cuboidal, and the zona pellucida forms around the oocyte. Secondary Follicle (Option B): The primary follicle grows larger, forming multiple layers of granulosa cells, and small fluid-filled spaces begin to appear. The theca interna and externa layers develop around the follicle. Tertiary Follicle (Antral Follicle): The secondary follicle further develops as the fluid-filled spaces coalesce to form an antrum . The granulosa cells form the cumulus oophorus surrounding the oocyte. Stages of Follicle Maturation: Primordial Follicle ↓ Primary Follicle ↓ Secondary Follicle ↓ Tertiary Follicle (Antral Follicle) ↓ Graafian Follicle (Mature Follicle) @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 27-week gestational-age preterm infant in the NICU experiences persistent apnea lasting over 20 seconds despite gentle tactile stimulation and supplemental oxygen. Nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) has been used but has not resolved the episodes. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.stemHtml: A 27-week gestational-age preterm infant in the NICU experiences persistent apnea lasting over 20 seconds despite gentle tactile stimulation and supplemental oxygen. Nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) has been used but has not resolved the episodes. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP)

questions.solution: citrate Explanation: Caffeine is the treatment of choice for recurrent or persistent apnea of prematurity that does not respond to initial measures like tactile stimulation or nCPAP. It increases central respiratory drive, lowers the threshold for response to hypercapnia, enhances diaphragmatic contractility, and prevents diaphragmatic fatigue. Management of Apnea of Prematurity: For mild and intermittent episodes: Gentle tactile stimulation or provision of supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula is often sufficient. If apnea episodes are more frequent or prolonged, nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) or heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula (HHHFNC) can be used to maintain airway patency. For recurrent or persistent apnea: Methylxanthines (e.g., caffeine) are preferred because they effectively stimulate respiratory drive and reduce the incidence and severity of apnea. Caffeine aids in extubation and lowers Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) risk with fewer side effects than theophylline. It is safe for oral or intravenous use with a wide therapeutic window and minimal need for serum monitoring. Continuing nCPAP (Option A) is beneficial for managing obstructive or mixed apnea by maintaining airway patency but is less effective for central apnea. Since the apnea persists despite nCPAP, additional pharmacological intervention is needed. Initiate doxapram infusion (Option C): Doxapram is a respiratory stimulant but is less commonly used due to side effects and is typically considered only if methylxanthines are ineffective. Start low-dose theophylline (Option D): Theophylline is another methylxanthine but is less preferred than caffeine due to a shorter half-life and higher risk of side effects d/t narrow therapeutic range (5-15 microgram), such as tachycardia and feeding intolerance. @Neet_pg_bot

  • It increases central respiratory drive, lowers the threshold for response to hypercapnia, enhances diaphragmatic contractility, and prevents diaphragmatic fatigue.

 

Management of Apnea of Prematurity:

  • For mild and intermittent episodes: Gentle tactile stimulation or provision of supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula is often sufficient.
  • If apnea episodes are more frequent or prolonged, nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) or heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula (HHHFNC) can be used to maintain airway patency.
  • For recurrent or persistent apnea:
    • Methylxanthines (e.g., caffeine) are preferred because they effectively stimulate respiratory drive and reduce the incidence and severity of apnea.
    • Caffeine aids in extubation and lowers Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) risk with fewer side effects than theophylline.
    • It is safe for oral or intravenous use with a wide therapeutic window and minimal need for serum monitoring.

 

Continuing nCPAP (Option A) is beneficial for managing obstructive or mixed apnea by maintaining airway patency but is less effective for central apnea. Since the apnea persists despite nCPAP, additional pharmacological intervention is needed.

 

Initiate doxapram infusion (Option C): Doxapram is a respiratory stimulant but is less commonly used due to side effects and is typically considered only if methylxanthines are ineffective.

 

Start low-dose theophylline (Option D): Theophylline is another methylxanthine but is less preferred than caffeine due to a shorter half-life and higher risk of side effects d/t narrow therapeutic range (5-15 microgram), such as tachycardia and feeding intolerance.

questions.stem: The image shows a 16 year old boy brought to the clinic by his father with an unusual pattern of hair loss. History states that he has become increasingly reclusive, avoiding family gatherings and showing less interest in his usual hobbies spending most of his time alone in his room. The boy himself appears unaware of the issue and has no complaints. What is the possible diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: The image shows a 16 year old boy brought to the clinic by his father with an unusual pattern of hair loss. History states that he has become increasingly reclusive, avoiding family gatherings and showing less interest in his usual hobbies spending most of his time alone in his room. The boy himself appears unaware of the issue and has no complaints. What is the possible diagnosis?
questions.solution: ng> The boy with the above history and a characteristic Friar Tuck hair loss pattern has trichotillomania. Trichotillomania: It is a psychiatric disorder in which obsessive, recurrent pulling of one’s hair results in hair loss. It is seen in adolescents or young adults, more commonly in girls. Patchy hair loss with broken hair of variable lengths is seen in commonly accessible sites like the frontoparietal area of the scalp. In the Friar Tuck sign or Tonsure pattern, there is uneven hair loss in a circular pattern with surrounding hairs remaining unaffected. Perifollicular hemorrhages can also be seen because of trauma to the scalp. Skin biopsy shows empty hair follicles, with some forming soft twisted hairs described as tracheomalacia. Treatment includes cognitive behavioral therapy and antipsychotic medications like SSRI and paroxetine. Trichobezoar/ Rapunzel syndrome is caused by chronic ingestion of hair ; it is commonly seen in young females who may have psychological disorders, such as trichophagia and trichotillomania. Common symptoms are abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Netherton syndrome (Option D) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the serine protease inhibitor. Characteristic triad includes, Congenital Ichtyosiform erythroderma. Trichorrhexis invaginata (Bamboo hair). Atopic diathesis. Alopecia areata (Option B) is an autoimmune condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks hair follicles, leading to sudden, round patches of hair loss. This is not consistent with the given clinical scenario. Pseudopelade of Brocq (Option C) is a chronic and slowly progressive idiopathic condition with no inflammation, scaling, or erythema. Smooth patches due to scarring alopecia. Footprint in snow appearance-spreading patches of cicatricial alopecia. @Neet_pg_bot

ng>

The boy with the above history and a characteristic Friar Tuck hair loss pattern has trichotillomania.

Trichotillomania:

  • It is a psychiatric disorder in which obsessive, recurrent pulling of one’s hair results in hair loss.
  • It is seen in adolescents or young adults, more commonly in girls.
  • Patchy hair loss with broken hair of variable lengths is seen in commonly accessible sites like the frontoparietal area of the scalp.
  • In the Friar Tuck sign or Tonsure pattern, there is uneven hair loss in a circular pattern with surrounding hairs remaining unaffected.

  • Perifollicular hemorrhages can also be seen because of trauma to the scalp.
  • Skin biopsy shows empty hair follicles, with some forming soft twisted hairs described as tracheomalacia.
  • Treatment includes cognitive behavioral therapy and antipsychotic medications like SSRI and paroxetine.
  • Trichobezoar/ Rapunzel syndrome is caused by chronic ingestion of hair; it is commonly seen in young females who may have psychological disorders, such as trichophagia and trichotillomania. Common symptoms are abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss.

Netherton syndrome (Option D) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the serine protease inhibitor. Characteristic triad includes,

  • Congenital Ichtyosiform erythroderma.
  • Trichorrhexis invaginata (Bamboo hair).
  • Atopic diathesis.

Alopecia areata (Option B) is an autoimmune condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks hair follicles, leading to sudden, round patches of hair loss. This is not consistent with the given clinical scenario.

Pseudopelade of Brocq (Option C) is a chronic and slowly progressive idiopathic condition with no inflammation, scaling, or erythema.

  • Smooth patches due to scarring alopecia.
  • Footprint in snow appearance-spreading patches of cicatricial alopecia.

Technology Utilizes 3D surface scanning, MSCT, MRI, and CAD photogrammetry to create a digital, objective record. (Option D) This can be shared online for secondary opinions and presented as evidence in court if required. Features Provides high-resolution, colored 3D images in various sections Allows visualization of body surfaces, deeper tissues, organs, coronary vessels, pulmonary emboli, soft tissue trauma, and bone injuries Limitations High cost of equipment Radiologic imaging limitations, interference from metal Limited ability to distinguish internal organ colors Incomplete database for diagnosis Challenges in identifying infection status , antemortem vs. postmortem wounds (Options B and C ruled out) Difficulty in identifying postmortem artifacts and subtle tissue injuries, and differentiating certain pathological conditions (Option D) Psychological autopsy - Meticulous collection of data after someone’s suicide to understand the circumstances of their death. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
h:612px">

Virtual autopsy/Virtopsy

Virtopsy is a non-invasive alternative to traditional autopsy using imaging instead of physical dissection.

Technology

  • Utilizes 3D surface scanning, MSCT, MRI, and CAD photogrammetry to create a digital, objective record. (Option D)
  • This can be shared online for secondary opinions and presented as evidence in court if required.

Features

  • Provides high-resolution, colored 3D images in various sections
  • Allows visualization of body surfaces, deeper tissues, organs, coronary vessels, pulmonary emboli, soft tissue trauma, and bone injuries

Limitations

  • High cost of equipment
  • Radiologic imaging limitations, interference from metal
  • Limited ability to distinguish internal organ colors
  • Incomplete database for diagnosis
  • Challenges in identifying infection status, antemortem vs. postmortem wounds (Options B and C ruled out)
  • Difficulty in identifying postmortem artifacts and subtle tissue injuries, and differentiating certain pathological conditions (Option D)

 

Psychological autopsy - Meticulous collection of data after someone’s suicide to understand the circumstances of their death.

What is the most likely finding on a biopsy from the lymph node?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old female presents with a history of weight loss, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and pleural effusion. HRCT shows a "tree-in-bud" appearance with lung consolidation and effusion. Pleural fluid analysis reveals low ADA levels and lymphocytic predominance. What is the most likely finding on a biopsy from the lymph node?
questions.solution: Clinical history plus CT findings plus lymphocytosis is highly suggestive of tuberculosis etiology. High Adenosine levels are diagnostic of pleural TB but low levels do not rule out TB. Fungal etiology in immunocompetent patient is highly unlikely. Answer is necrotizing epithelioid granuloma which is characteristic finding of TB. High endemicity of TB is another reason for favoring this option. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: ta" data-dictid="74dd17aa171692777200dcc186c177">trinucleotide repeat disorder, seen in the axon region of a gene present on chromosome 4. HD is characterised by the Anticipation/Sherman Paradox. The number of repeats increases with every generation, leading to early and more severe presentation in the next generation. HD features psychiatric disturbances and choreoathetosis early on, with cognitive disturbance and death later. Examples of diseases showing anticipation include: Autosomal Dominant Autosomal Recessive Multiple spinocerebellar ataxias Huntington’s disease – CAG repeats Myotonic dystrophy – CTG Congenital dyskeratosis – TTAGGG (telomere repeating sequence) Friedreich’s ataxia – GAA X-linked Fragile X Syndrome – CGG Others Crohn’s disease Behcet’s disease Mosaicism (Option B) refers to the presence of multiple genetically different cell lines in the same individual. Imprinting (Option C) refers to a gene silencing. Non-penetrance (Option D): It means that the Gene is received from parents but no symptoms are seen in patient. @Neet_pg_bot

The data collected over a month is as follows: Ward Patients with infections Patients without infections Total General 20 80 100 Intensive Care 30 70 100 Pediatric 10 90 100 Total 60 240 300 Using the Chi-Square test, what is the expected number of patients with infections in the General Ward if there is no association between the ward type and infection status?

questions.solution: p> Explanation: The expected number for each cell in a Chi-square test is calculated by multiplying the row total by the column total and dividing by the grand total. The formula for the expected frequency in a cell is: E=(Row Total)×(Column Total) / Grand Total For the General ward and infections: = (Total patients in General ward x Total patients with infections) / Total number of patients = (100 x 60) / 300 = 6000 / 300 = 20 @Neet_pg_bot

The formula for the expected frequency in a cell is: E=(Row Total)×(Column Total) / Grand Total

For the General ward and infections:

= (Total patients in General ward x Total patients with infections) / Total number of patients

= (100 x 60) / 300

= 6000 / 300

= 20

questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks of gestation presents for a routine prenatal visit. She reports no pain, contractions, or bleeding. An ultrasound performed at 20 weeks showed a placenta previa that remained stable on follow-up ultrasound. What should be the next step in the management of this patient?

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.answerText: Expectant management with periodic transvaginal ultrasounds (TVS) and implementation of the McAfee Johnson regimen
questions.solution: nagement involves expectant management in a stable case of placenta previa with no active bleeding or other complications. This includes periodic Transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) monitoring and following the McAfee and Johnson regimen. McAfee and Johnson regime: It is an expectant management strategy for patients with placenta previa to ensure maternal and fetal safety while aiming to prolong the pregnancy. Indications: The mother is healthy (Hb >10 g % and haematocrit > 30%). Absence of active vaginal bleeding. Gestational age <37 weeks. Reactive CTG. Steps in McAfee and Johnson regime: Hospitalise the patient (Bed rest). Monitoring: Maternal vitals. Fetal heart sounds. Bleeding. Arrange for blood. If the patient is Rh (-ve), anti-D should be given. Injection of corticosteroids to hasten lung maturity of the fetus. Short-term tocolytic (nifedipine) should be provided if any contractions are present. If pregnancy <32 weeks: MgSO 4 (neural protection). The above-mentioned steps are continued till 37 weeks, after which elective cesarean section can be done. Immediate hospitalisation and preparation for emergency C-section (Option A) : No need for now since no bleeding, pain or contractions. Administration of magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection and immediate delivery (Option C): MgSO4 only in case of extreme preterms and no indication for immediate delivery for now. Routine follow-up with monthly abdominal ultrasounds without activity restrictions (Option D): No need of monthly scans and it is advised to avoid exertion. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
nagement involves expectant management in a stable case of placenta previa with no active bleeding or other complications. This includes periodic Transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) monitoring and following the McAfee and Johnson regimen.

 

McAfee and Johnson regime:

It is an expectant management strategy for patients with placenta previa to ensure maternal and fetal safety while aiming to prolong the pregnancy.

 

Indications:
  • The mother is healthy (Hb >10 g % and haematocrit > 30%).
  • Absence of active vaginal bleeding.
  • Gestational age <37 weeks.
  • Reactive CTG.

Steps in McAfee and Johnson regime:
  1. Hospitalise the patient (Bed rest).
  2. Monitoring:
    1. Maternal vitals.
    2. Fetal heart sounds.
    3. Bleeding.
  3. Arrange for blood.
  4. If the patient is Rh (-ve), anti-D should be given.
  5. Injection of corticosteroids to hasten lung maturity of the fetus.
  6. Short-term tocolytic (nifedipine) should be provided if any contractions are present.
  7. If pregnancy <32 weeks: MgSO4 (neural protection).
 

The above-mentioned steps are continued till 37 weeks, after which elective cesarean section can be done.

 

Immediate hospitalisation and preparation for emergency C-section (Option A): No need for now since no bleeding, pain or contractions.

Administration of magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection and immediate delivery (Option C): MgSO4 only in case of extreme preterms and no indication for immediate delivery for now. 

Routine follow-up with monthly abdominal ultrasounds without activity restrictions (Option D): No need of monthly scans and it is advised to avoid exertion.

questions.solution: The involvement of epiglottis in laryngeal carcinoma is indicative of supraglottic laryngeal carcinoma , in which nodal metastases occur early and are commonly bilateral. Supraglottic Laryngeal Carcinoma: Incidence Less frequent than glottic cancer; about 30-35% of all laryngeal cancers Site Majority on epiglottis, false cords, followed by aryepiglottic folds Vocal cord involvement Usually late; vocal cords often spared in early stages Lymphatic spread Early and often bilateral Upper and middle jugular nodes commonly involved Cancer of infrahyoid epiglottis & anterior ventricular band may extend into pre-epiglottic space (Option D) Symptoms Early: Often silent, dysphagia, throat pain Late: Hoarseness, weight loss, respiratory obstruction, halitosis (Option B) Histopathology 90-95% squamous cell carcinoma (Option C) Others include verrucous carcinoma, spindle cell carcinoma Highly anaplastic Prognosis Generally worse than glottic cancer due to: Late diagnosis High rate & early lymph node metastasis Anaplastic nature @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The involvement of epiglottis in laryngeal carcinoma is indicative of supraglottic laryngeal carcinoma, in which nodal metastases occur early and are commonly bilateral.

Supraglottic Laryngeal Carcinoma:

Incidence

Less frequent than glottic cancer; about 30-35% of all laryngeal cancers

Site

Majority on epiglottis, false cords, followed by aryepiglottic folds

Vocal cord involvement

Usually late; vocal cords often spared in early stages

Lymphatic spread
  • Early and often bilateral
  • Upper and middle jugular nodes commonly involved
  • Cancer of infrahyoid epiglottis & anterior ventricular band may extend into pre-epiglottic space (Option D)

Symptoms
  • Early: Often silent, dysphagia, throat pain
  • Late: Hoarseness, weight loss, respiratory obstruction, halitosis (Option B)

Histopathology
  • 90-95% squamous cell carcinoma (Option C)
  • Others include verrucous carcinoma, spindle cell carcinoma
  • Highly anaplastic

Prognosis

Generally worse than glottic cancer due to:

  • Late diagnosis
  • High rate & early lymph node metastasis
  • Anaplastic nature

Olfactory Neuroblastoma (Esthesioneuroblastoma): Originates from the Olfactory Epithelium in the upper third of the nasal cavity which is characterised by neuroblastic differentiation and can be locally aggressive with a tendency to invade adjacent structures. Bimodal peaks of incidence (10-20 years & 50-60 years) Symptoms: Early Symptoms: Unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis (nosebleeds). Advanced Symptoms: Tumour invades the orbit or surrounding structures, causing proptosis, headache, epiphora, diplopia, and blurred vision. Metastasis: Lymph node metastases in the neck can occur in 10-15% of cases. Diagnosis: Intranasal or Endoscopic Examination: Reveals a friable, cherry-red, polypoidal mass Highly vascular, so biopsy should be preceded by imaging studies. Imaging Studies: CT Scan: Shows tumour extent, and possible erosion of cribriform plate/orbital wall. MRI: Detects orbital or intracranial extension. Biopsy: Confirms the tumour type; it may be low-grade with pseudorosette formation or high-grade with nuclear pleomorphism but no rosette formation. Treatment: Craniofacial resection, with or without preoperative radiation or chemotherapy, followed by adjuvant radiation for advanced cases. Staging Systems: Kadish Staging System (with Morita’s Modification): Stage A Tumour limited to the nasal cavity. Stage B Tumour involving the nasal cavity and sinuses. Stage C Tumour extending beyond the nasal and paranasal sinuses. Stage D Tumor with metastasis to cervical nodes or distant sites. Other Staging Systems: Morita’s Staging System Dulguerov and Calcaterra Staging System Breslow Classification (Option B) is used for staging melanoma based on the thickness of the tumor. Different Types of Capnographic Waveforms: A normal wave in controlled mechanical ventilation Normal wave during spontaneous breathing Bronchospasm (asthma, COPD exacerbation) / partially obstructed ET tube or breathing circuit Shark fin appearance Spontaneous breathing effort during controlled mechanical ventilation (Curare notch) Curare cleft, or notch, is seen during spontaneous ventilation. Esophageal intubation can initially produce an EtCO2 due to gastric CO2 however this should taper after a few breaths. Right main-stem intubation may still have a normal EtCO2, so get a CXR to confirm optimal tube positioning. Role during Cardiac Arrest: EtCO2 > 20 suggests good quality CPR. If it starts to drop, consider switching compressors or making sure the LUCUS is in the appropriate position. A sudden increase in EtCO2 greater than 10 from the patient’s baseline can be an early indication of ROSC. questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a severe migraine headache that has been ongoing for several hours. She reports that her headache is accompanied by nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia. She has tried over-the-counter pain relievers without relief. What medication would you prescribe to help alleviate her symptoms?
questions.solution: an is a more potent and specific migraine treatment that provides superior pain relief than paracetamol. Mechanism of Action It is a selective 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonist that activates other subtypes of 5-HT1 receptors only at very high concentrations. Inhibits the release of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and causes cranial vasoconstriction. Administration and Efficacy It is administered at the onset of a migraine attack and is as effective and better tolerated than ergotamine. About 3/4 of patients obtain complete or significant relief within 2-3 hours. Available in various formulations such as Oral tablets, Nasal sprays, Injections, and Rectal suppositories. questions.solution: > This is a case of Secondary postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) , also known as a delayed or late puerperal hemorrhage , which occurs between 24 hours and 12 weeks after delivery. Clinically significant uterine bleeding occurs in about 1% of women, usually within 1 to 2 weeks of delivery. Uterine atony is the failure of the uterus to contract effectively after delivery and is the most common cause of primary PPH (occurring within the first 24 hours postpartum). It leads to excessive bleeding immediately after birth rather than delayed bleeding. This patient's presentation on postpartum day 10 makes uterine atony an unlikely cause of her current symptoms. Secondary Postpartum Hemorrhage Cause Description Retained Placental Fragments and Membranes (Option A) Most common cause They can prevent proper uterine involution and healing, leading to significant bleeding. Rarely, retained products undergo necrosis and fibrin deposition, forming a placental polyp that can cause severe hemorrhage. Infection Tissue breakdown and delayed healing Endometritis (Option C) Inflammation of the uterine lining and delayed healing. Symptoms typically include fever, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia. Subinvolution of Placental Site Uterus's failure to return to its normal size after delivery. When the placental site heals slowly, it can increase the risk of secondary bleeding Uterine artery Pseudoaneurysm (Option D) A severe but rare cause of secondary PPH. It occurs when a pseudoaneurysm forms in the uterine artery, leading to delayed hemorrhage. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Explanation: This patient's symptoms, combined with her recent history of diverticulitis, point towards a pelvic abscess. Clinical Features of Pelvic Abscess: Lower abdominal pain and tenderness due to pus accumulation. Fever accompanied by chills and rigor. Pus irritates the anterior rectal wall (since the pouch of Douglas is in contact with this area) causing multiple episodes of loose stools with mucus. Digital rectal examination may reveal a bulge on the anterior wall of the rectum. Investigation: Initial investigation: Ultrasound. Investigation of choice: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT). Management: If a clean window is present: Percutaneous aspiration guided by ultrasound or CT (preferred treatment) is performed. If no clean window is available due to bowel loops adhering to the abscess cavity: For females: Posterior colpotomy through the posterior vaginal wall (in close contact with the pouch of Douglas). For males: Anterior rectal drainage through the anterior rectal wall. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: During induction of anesthesia, a patient receiving etomidate shows an increase in blood pressure and heart rate. How does etomidate primarily achieve cardiovascular stability?
questions.stemHtml: During induction of anesthesia, a patient receiving etomidate shows an increase in blood pressure and heart rate. How does etomidate primarily achieve cardiovascular stability?

options.label: A
options.text: By activating the sympathetic nervous system

questions.solution: which increases blood pressure and contributes to cardiovascular stability by preventing excessive sympathetic stimulation . Effects of Etomidate on the Cardiovascular System Hemodynamic Stability : Etomidate maintains hemodynamic stability by not affecting the sympathetic nervous system or baroreceptor function. (Option A & B) Blood Pressure Effects : Activation of α2-adrenoceptors leads to increased blood pressure, contributing to cardiovascular stability during anesthesia induction. Comparison with Other Anesthetics : Minimal cardiovascular effects distinguish etomidate from other rapid-onset anesthetics, making it suitable for patients with heart conditions. Patient Suitability : Effective for patients with valvular or ischemic heart disease and those with poor cardiac function during non cardiac surgeries. Hemodynamic Responses : Etomidate may lead to more hypertension and tachycardia compared to propofol during induction. Oxygen Supply and Demand : Maintains a stable myocardial oxygen supply-to-demand ratio . (Option D) Analgesic Considerations : Lacks analgesic properties; should be combined with opioids to manage hemodynamic changes during laryngoscopy and intubation. Advantages in Hemorrhagic Shock : In cases of hemorrhagic shock, etomidate's pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics remain largely unchanged, making it advantageous for induction. @Neet_pg_bot

which increases blood pressure and contributes to cardiovascular stability by preventing excessive sympathetic stimulation.

Effects of Etomidate on the Cardiovascular System

  • Hemodynamic Stability:

  • Blood Pressure Effects:

questions.stem: Which of the following is a pathognomonic feature of a lightning strike injury?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a pathognomonic feature of a lightning strike injury?
questions.solution: ng>Lichtenberg flowers: These are characteristic fern-like patterns that appear on the skin following a lightning strike. Lightning stroke Lightning bolt(DC>1000 million V) is produced when the charged undersurface of a thundercloud sends its electrical charge to the ground. Death is caused by high voltage current due to cardiopulmonary arrest or electrothermal injuries. Lichtenberg flowers/Arborescent markings: Pathognomic feature of lightning strike. Superficial, several inches long, thin, irregular, tortuous, dendritic red marks on the skin having resemblance to the branches of a tree. This Fern-like pattern of erythema in the skin is usually found over the shoulders or flanks. Appears within 1hr and disappears in 24-48 hrs if person survives. Other features of lightning strike: Development of edema of skin at the point of entry wound. Linear burns and surface burns Fusing and magnetisation of metallic articles. Contusions, lacerations, rupture of tympanic membrane. Singed hair and patterned skin burns marks underneath metal articles of jewellery. Joule burns (Option B): These are burns caused by the conversion of electrical energy into heat within the body and are not specific to lightning strikes. They can occur in any electrical injury. Crocodile skin lesions (Option C): These are indicative of other types of electrical injuries, characterized by a specific pattern of skin damage but are not unique to lightning strikes. Sparrow foot marks (Option D): Peculiar facial lacerations due to contact with the shattered windscreen seen in transportation injuries. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ng>Lichtenberg flowers: These are characteristic fern-like patterns that appear on the skin following a lightning strike.

 

Lightning stroke

  • Lightning bolt(DC>1000 million V) is produced when the charged undersurface of a thundercloud sends its electrical charge to the ground.
  • Death is caused by high voltage current due to cardiopulmonary arrest or electrothermal injuries.

 

Lichtenberg flowers/Arborescent markings:

  • Pathognomic feature of lightning strike.
  • Superficial, several inches long, thin, irregular, tortuous, dendritic red marks on the skin having resemblance to the branches of a tree.
  • This Fern-like pattern of erythema in the skin is usually found over the shoulders or flanks.
  • Appears within 1hr and disappears in 24-48 hrs if person survives.

 

 

 

Other features of lightning strike:

  • Development of edema of skin at the point of entry wound.
  • Linear burns and surface burns
  • Fusing and magnetisation of metallic articles.
  • Contusions, lacerations, rupture of tympanic membrane.
  • Singed hair and patterned skin burns marks underneath metal articles of jewellery.

Joule burns (Option B): These are burns caused by the conversion of electrical energy into heat within the body and are not specific to lightning strikes. They can occur in any electrical injury.

 

Crocodile skin lesions (Option C): These are indicative of other types of electrical injuries, characterized by a specific pattern of skin damage but are not unique to lightning strikes.

 

Sparrow foot marks (Option D): Peculiar facial lacerations due to contact with the shattered windscreen seen in transportation injuries.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female patient with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has started on clozapine. What is the appropriate duration and frequency of blood test monitoring for this patient taking clozapine?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old female patient with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has started on clozapine. What is the appropriate duration and frequency of blood test monitoring for this patient taking clozapine?

options.label: A
options.text: Weekly for 6 months, bi-weekly for 6 months, then monthly.

options.label: B
options.text: Monthly for 6 months, then every 3 months.

options.label: C
options.text: Weekly for 3 months, bi-weekly for 3 months, then monthly.

options.label: D
options.text: Monthly for 1 year, then every 6 months.

questions.answerText: Weekly for 6 months, bi-weekly for 6 months, then monthly.
questions.solution: ozapine is associated with a risk of agranulocytosis , especially during the first year of treatment. Regular monitoring of Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) is mandatory to detect early neutropenia or agranulocytosis. The standard hematological monitoring schedule for patients on clozapine is: Weekly for the first 6 months Every 2 weeks (bi-weekly) for the next 6 months Monthly after 1 year , if ANC remains stable Monitoring Phase Frequency Duration Initial phase Weekly First 6 months Intermediate Bi-weekly Next 6 months Maintenance Monthly After 1 year, lifelong while on clozapine Monthly for 6 months, then every 3 months (Option B): This monitoring frequency is dangerously infrequent for clozapine, especially during the crucial initial months, and does not meet safety guidelines for agranulocytosis risk. Weekly for 3 months, bi-weekly for 3 months, then monthly (Option C): This option has an insufficient duration of intensified weekly and bi-weekly monitoring (only 3 months each), leaving patients at higher risk for undetected agranulocytosis compared to the standard 6-month periods. Monthly for 1 year, then every 6 months (Option D): This schedule is grossly inadequate for clozapine safety monitoring, particularly during the critical first year, and would not allow for timely detection of severe neutropenia or agranulocytosis. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ozapine is associated with a risk of agranulocytosis, especially during the first year of treatment.

  • Regular monitoring of Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) is mandatory to detect early neutropenia or agranulocytosis.

  • The standard hematological monitoring schedule for patients on clozapine is:

    • Weekly for the first 6 months

    • Every 2 weeks (bi-weekly) for the next 6 months

    • Monthly after 1 year, if ANC remains stable

    • Monitoring Phase Frequency Duration
    Initial phase Weekly First 6 months
    Intermediate Bi-weekly Next 6 months
    Maintenance Monthly After 1 year, lifelong while on clozapine

     

    Monthly for 6 months, then every 3 months (Option B): This monitoring frequency is dangerously infrequent for clozapine, especially during the crucial initial months, and does not meet safety guidelines for agranulocytosis risk.

    Weekly for 3 months, bi-weekly for 3 months, then monthly (Option C): This option has an insufficient duration of intensified weekly and bi-weekly monitoring (only 3 months each), leaving patients at higher risk for undetected agranulocytosis compared to the standard 6-month periods.

    Monthly for 1 year, then every 6 months (Option D): This schedule is grossly inadequate for clozapine safety monitoring, particularly during the critical first year, and would not allow for timely detection of severe neutropenia or agranulocytosis.

questions.stem: A physiologist is studying blood flow in a network of four parallel blood vessels. The effective resistance of the network of vessels is 4.8 R units. The pressure at the proximal end of the network is 150 mmHg, and the pressure at the distal end is 90 mmHg. What is the total blood flow rate through the network of vessels?
questions.stemHtml: A physiologist is studying blood flow in a network of four parallel blood vessels. The effective resistance of the network of vessels is 4.8 R units. The pressure at the proximal end of the network is 150 mmHg, and the pressure at the distal end is 90 mmHg. What is the total blood flow rate through the network of vessels?
questions.solution: Effective Perfusion Pressure = 150 mmHg − 90 mmHg= 60 mmHg Using the blood flow analogue of Ohm's law: Blood flow (F) in any part of the circulatory system is determined by the effective perfusion pressure (P) and the resistance (R) it encounters: F = P/R 𝑅 total = 4.8R units Flow = Pressure / Resistance = 60/4.8 =12.5 L/s @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• Effective Perfusion Pressure = 150 mmHg − 90 mmHg= 60 mmHg
  • Using the blood flow analogue of Ohm's law: Blood flow (F) in any part of the circulatory system is determined by the effective perfusion pressure (P) and the resistance (R) it encounters: F = P/R
    • 𝑅 total = 4.8R units
    • Flow = Pressure / Resistance = 60/4.8 =12.5 L/s

questions.stem: A 38-year-old female with a history of chronic kidney disease presents with persistent fatigue, bone pain, and muscle weakness. Blood work reveals elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP), high serum phosphorus, and low serum calcium. What will the result of 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D likely reveal?
questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old female with a history of chronic kidney disease presents with persistent fatigue, bone pain, and muscle weakness. Blood work reveals elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP), high serum phosphorus, and low serum calcium. What will the result of 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D likely reveal?

options.label: B
options.text: Estimating 1, 25 dihydroxy vitamin D is unnecessary.

questions.solution: Patients with CKD often have reduced 1α-hydroxylase, leading to lower levels of active vitamin D: 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D. 1,25 dihydroxy Vitamin D in Chronic kidney disease: In chronic kidney disease (CKD), estimating 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D levels is essential due to the kidneys' role in vitamin D metabolism. (Option B ruled out) The kidneys are the primary site where 1α-hydroxylase converts inactive vitamin D (25 hydroxy cholecalciferol) into its active form, 1,25 dihydroxy cholecalciferol. Patients with CKD often have reduced 1α-hydroxylase, leading to lower levels of active vitamin D: 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D. (Options A and D ruled out) Impact on Calcium Homeostasis : Low levels in CKD causes hypocalcemia. Secondary Hyperparathyroidism : To compensate for low calcium, PTH increases and has negative consequences for bone health. Renal Osteodystrophy : Abnormal bone turnover, as evidenced by the elevated alkaline phosphatase in the clinical scenario. Diagnostic Value : 1,25 dihydroxy cholecalciferol has a longer half-life and remains stable. Therefore, it provides a more reliable test for vitamin D status in CKD and helps guide appropriate treatment. Treatment: Dialysis. Calcimimetic drugs - Cinacalcet and Etelcalcetide. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Patients with CKD often have reduced 1α-hydroxylase, leading to lower levels of active vitamin D: 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D.

1,25 dihydroxy Vitamin D in Chronic kidney disease:

  • In chronic kidney disease (CKD), estimating 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D levels is essential due to the kidneys' role in vitamin D metabolism. (Option B ruled out)
  • The kidneys are the primary site where 1α-hydroxylase converts inactive vitamin D (25 hydroxy cholecalciferol) into its active form, 1,25 dihydroxy cholecalciferol.
  • Patients with CKD often have reduced 1α-hydroxylase, leading to lower levels of active vitamin D: 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D. (Options A and D ruled out)
  • Impact on Calcium Homeostasis: Low levels in CKD causes hypocalcemia.
  • Secondary Hyperparathyroidism: To compensate for low calcium, PTH increases and has negative consequences for bone health.
  • Renal Osteodystrophy: Abnormal bone turnover, as evidenced by the elevated alkaline phosphatase in the clinical scenario.
  • Diagnostic Value: 1,25 dihydroxy cholecalciferol has a longer half-life and remains stable. Therefore, it provides a more reliable test for vitamin D status in CKD and helps guide appropriate treatment.
  • Treatment:
    • Dialysis.
    • Calcimimetic drugs - Cinacalcet and Etelcalcetide.
