questions.stem: Correctly match the following statements with True(T)/ False(F) 1) Continuity is disrupted in tangentiality 2) Goal is not reached in circumstantiality 3) Perseveration is associated with organic mental disorder 4) Continuity is preserved in perseveration 5) Thought blocking is associated with schizophrenia
questions.solution: >1) Continuity is maintained in tangentiality 2) Goal is reached in circumstantiality 3) Perseveration is associated with organic mental disorder 4) Continuity is disrupted in perseveration 5) Thought blocking is associated with schizophrenia Hence, 1-F , 2-F , 3-T , 4-F , 5-T is the correct answer. Disorders of flow/stream of thought: Continuity maintained with increased speed: Flight of ideas: rapid flow of ideas from one to another, connected and partially understandable Prolixity: Milder form of flight of ideas Clang association: sentences with rhyming Continuity maintained with decreased speed: (Statement-1) Thought slowing/retardation: Decrease in speed of thought, seen in depression Circumstantiality: Overinclusion of trivial and unnecessary details, but ultimately reaches the answer. (Statement-2) Tangentiality: Flow of irrelevant thoughts that deviates from the main topic and never reaches the answer. Continuity disrupted: Perseveration: (Statement-4) Same thought persists beyond the point of relevance. Pathological repetition of the same response to different stimuli. Seen in organic mental disorder (Statement-3) and schizophrenia. Thought blocking: Sudden arrest of thought and then the person resumes with an entirely new thought. Seen in schizophrenia. (Statement-5) @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
>1) Continuity is maintained in tangentiality

2) Goal is reached in circumstantiality

3) Perseveration is associated with organic mental disorder

4) Continuity is disrupted in perseveration

5) Thought blocking is associated with schizophrenia

Hence, 1-F,2-F,3-T,4-F,5-T is the correct answer.

Disorders of flow/stream of thought:

Continuity maintained with increased speed:
  • Flight of ideas: rapid flow of ideas from one to another, connected and partially understandable
  • Prolixity: Milder form of flight of ideas
  • Clang association: sentences with rhyming

Continuity maintained with decreased speed: (Statement-1)
  • Thought slowing/retardation: Decrease in speed of thought, seen in depression
  • Circumstantiality: Overinclusion of trivial and unnecessary details, but ultimately reaches the answer. (Statement-2)
  • Tangentiality: Flow of irrelevant thoughts that deviates from the main topic and never reaches the answer.

Continuity disrupted:

  • Perseveration: (Statement-4)
    • Same thought persists beyond the point of relevance.
    • Pathological repetition of the same response to different stimuli.
    • Seen in organic mental disorder (Statement-3) and schizophrenia.
  • Thought blocking:
    • Sudden arrest of thought and then the person resumes with an entirely new thought.
    • Seen in schizophrenia. (Statement-5)

questions.stem: Consider the following statements: i) f IPV is a live attenuated vaccine. ii) fIPV is not effective in control of epidemics iii) OPV has a shorter shelf life than IPV iv) fIPV provides humoral immunity only v) 5 ml of fIPV is administered via IM route Which of the following are correct?
questions.stemHtml:
Consider the following statements:
i) f IPV is a live attenuated vaccine.
ii) fIPV is not effective in control of epidemics
iii) OPV has a shorter shelf life than IPV
iv) fIPV provides humoral immunity only
v) 5 ml of fIPV is administered via IM route
Which of the following are correct?
questions.solution: i) IPV is a live attenuated vaccine: Incorrect IPV (Inactivated Poliovirus Vaccine) is a killed (inactivated) vaccine. ii) fIPV is not effective in control of epidemics: Correct Fractional IPV (fIPV) is not ideal for rapid outbreak control because it does not induce sufficient mucosal immunity , which is required for halting poliovirus transmission. OPV is preferred in epidemic situations due to its ability to induce gut immunity and stop transmission. iii) OPV has a shorter shelf life than IPV: Correct OPV is a live virus vaccine , requiring strict cold chain maintenance and has a shorter shelf life than IPV, which is inactivated and more stable. iv) fIPV provides humoral immunity only: Correct fIPV induces humoral (systemic) immunity but does not provide strong mucosal immunity in the intestines, which is necessary to prevent virus shedding. OPV provides both humoral and mucosal immunity. v) 5 ml of fIPV is administered via IM route: Incorrect fIPV is given as 0.1 ml intradermally , not 5 ml intramuscularly . The standard full-dose IPV (not fractional) is given intramuscularly (IM) . Differences Between IPV and OPV Feature IPV (Inactivated Poliovirus Vaccine) OPV (Oral Poliovirus Vaccine) Type of Vaccine Inactivated (killed) virus Live attenuated virus Route of Administration Intramuscular (IM) or Intradermal (ID) Oral (drops) Immunity Provided Systemic (humoral) immunity Systemic + mucosal immunity (gut immunity) Effectiveness in Epidemics Not effective in stopping transmission Highly effective in epidemic control Prevention of Virus Shedding Limited effect on intestinal virus shedding Strong gut immunity prevents shedding Shelf Life & Storage More stable, longer shelf life Less stable, requires strict cold chain Risk of Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV) No risk of VDPV Small risk of VDPV due to live virus reversion Use in Eradication Programs Primarily used in polio-free areas Used in endemic and outbreak settings @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• i) IPV is a live attenuated vaccine: Incorrect

    • IPV (Inactivated Poliovirus Vaccine) is a killed (inactivated) vaccine.

  • ii) fIPV is not effective in control of epidemics: Correct

    • Fractional IPV (fIPV) is not ideal for rapid outbreak control because it does not induce sufficient mucosal immunity, which is required for halting poliovirus transmission.

    • OPV is preferred in epidemic situations due to its ability to induce gut immunity and stop transmission.

  • iii) OPV has a shorter shelf life than IPV: Correct

    • OPV is a live virus vaccine, requiring strict cold chain maintenance and has a shorter shelf life than IPV, which is inactivated and more stable.

  • iv) fIPV provides humoral immunity only: Correct

    • fIPV induces humoral (systemic) immunity but does not provide strong mucosal immunity in the intestines, which is necessary to prevent virus shedding.

    • OPV provides both humoral and mucosal immunity.

  • v) 5 ml of fIPV is administered via IM route: Incorrect

    • fIPV is given as 0.1 ml intradermally, not 5 ml intramuscularly.

    • The standard full-dose IPV (not fractional) is given intramuscularly (IM).

    • Differences Between IPV and OPV

    Feature IPV (Inactivated Poliovirus Vaccine) OPV (Oral Poliovirus Vaccine)
    Type of Vaccine Inactivated (killed) virus Live attenuated virus
    Route of Administration Intramuscular (IM) or Intradermal (ID) Oral (drops)
    Immunity Provided Systemic (humoral) immunity Systemic + mucosal immunity (gut immunity)
    Effectiveness in Epidemics Not effective in stopping transmission Highly effective in epidemic control
    Prevention of Virus Shedding Limited effect on intestinal virus shedding Strong gut immunity prevents shedding
    Shelf Life & Storage More stable, longer shelf life Less stable, requires strict cold chain
    Risk of Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV) No risk of VDPV Small risk of VDPV due to live virus reversion
    Use in Eradication Programs Primarily used in polio-free areas Used in endemic and outbreak settings

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman, postmenopausal for the past 5 years, presents with a complaint of intermittent episodes of vaginal bleeding over the last month. Pelvic ultrasound reveals an endometrial thickness of 6 mm. What is the most appropriate investigation for evaluating postmenopausal bleeding in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 56-year-old woman, postmenopausal for the past 5 years, presents with a complaint of intermittent episodes of vaginal bleeding over the last month. Pelvic ultrasound reveals an endometrial thickness of 6 mm. What is the most appropriate investigation for evaluating postmenopausal bleeding in this patient?
questions.solution: >In a postmenopausal woman presenting with postmenopausal bleeding, with an endometrial thickness of 6 mm on ultrasound, the most appropriate investigation is an endometrial biopsy. It is the most definitive method to diagnose endometrial hyperplasia, polyps, or cancer in postmenopausal women with bleeding and increased endometrial thickness. Investigation approach in Post-menopausal bleeding: History and examination to be done. Transvaginal ultrasound should be done if the cervix looks normal, which is the first step in diagnosis. A 4 mm or greater endometrial thickness in postmenopausal women is considered abnormal. It requires further evaluation since there is an increased chance of endometrial hyperplasia, and cancer rises with increasing endometrial thickness. If growth/lesion is present in the cervix, a cervical biopsy should be done to rule out cervical malignancy. Repeat pelvic ultrasound in 3 months (Option A): Delaying further investigation is not appropriate because postmenopausal bleeding requires timely evaluation to rule out malignancy or other significant pathology. The sinusoidal pattern, describing a smooth, regular fetal heart rate oscillation is associated with severe fetal anaemia or maternal opioid use

A sinusoidal pattern in a cardiotocography (CTG) trace resembles a sine wave, with a stable fetal heart rate (FHR) and fixed or absent baseline variability lasting more than 30 minutes. Accelerations are absent in a true sinusoidal pattern. This pattern is often associated with:

  • Fetal anaemia
  • Fetomaternal haemorrhage
  • Vasa Previa
  • Fetal hypoxia (acidosis)

A sinusoidal pattern can also occur when the mother has been given narcotics.

The pseudo sinusoidal pattern shows a 'saw-toothed' pattern. It differs from the true sinusoidal pattern because it indicates a well-oxygenated fetus.

Acceleration pattern (Option A): Reassuring fetal status
Saltatory pattern (Option B): Sign of fetal distress
Variable deceleration pattern (Option D): Linked to umbilical cord compression

questions.solution: Tetany is primarily caused by a decrease in extracellular ionized calcium (Ca2+). This reduction increases the excitability of nerve and muscle cells, leading to symptoms such as muscle spasms and laryngospasm. Tetany: It is characterized by extensive skeletal muscle spasms Cause: Decrease in extracellular ionized calcium (Ca2+), leading to increased excitability of nerve and muscle cells. questions.solutionHtml:
Tetany is primarily caused by a decrease in extracellular ionized calcium (Ca2+). This reduction increases the excitability of nerve and muscle cells, leading to symptoms such as muscle spasms and laryngospasm.

 

Tetany:

  • It is characterized by extensive skeletal muscle spasms
  • Cause: Decrease in extracellular ionized calcium (Ca2+), leading to increased excitability of nerve and muscle cells.
  • Mechanism:

Increased Excitability: Reduced extracellular Ca2+ lowers its binding to voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve and muscle cells.

Action Potential Generation: Lower Ca2+ binding decreases the activation threshold of these channels, making them more likely to open and trigger action potentials.

  • Complication: Laryngospasm can obstruct the airway and potentially cause fatal asphyxia.

 

Calcium and Tetany:

  • Normal Total Calcium Levels: Total calcium might appear normal, but a decrease in ionized calcium can still cause tetany.
  • Influence of pH: Increased pH (alkalosis) from hyperventilation increases plasma protein ionization, binding more Ca2+ and reducing free Ca2+ availability.

 

Signs of Tetany:

  • Chvostek Sign: Contraction of facial muscles upon tapping the facial nerve.
  • Trousseau Sign: Spasm of upper extremity muscles, causing wrist and thumb flexion with finger extension; elicited by occluding circulation with a blood pressure cuff.

inus is an air-filled cavity located in the frontal bone. The frontal sinus drains through the frontonasal duct into the infundibulum and finally into the middle meatus.

 

Contents and Cells Around the Frontal Sinus:

ominate in vaginal cytology under the influence of estrogen. This is typically seen during the proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle when estrogen levels are high.

Neonatal Hepatitis: It refers to inflammation of the liver in newborns, typically presenting within the first few weeks of life. Etiology: Causes include viral infections (e.g., cytomegalovirus, rubella, hepatitis B), metabolic disorders, genetic conditions, and idiopathic origins. Clinical Presentation: Jaundice, hepatomegaly, dark urine, and poor weight gain.The disease can present as either mild or severe, with the potential for liver failure in severe cases. Explanation:

The given image shows normal filling of gallbladder and excretion of radioisotope into the intestine, suggesting neonatal hepatitis.

 

Neonatal Hepatitis:

It refers to inflammation of the liver in newborns, typically presenting within the first few weeks of life.

 

Etiology: Causes include viral infections (e.g., cytomegalovirus, rubella, hepatitis B), metabolic disorders, genetic conditions, and idiopathic origins.

 

Clinical Presentation: Jaundice, hepatomegaly, dark urine, and poor weight gain.The disease can present as either mild or severe, with the potential for liver failure in severe cases.

 

Diagnosis: Diagnosed through a combination of clinical evaluation, liver function tests (elevated ALT, AST), and specific serologic and metabolic tests.

  • HIDA: Shows normal excretion of radioisotope into the intestine.
  • Liver biopsy may show giant cell transformation, indicative of neonatal hepatitis.

 

Differential Diagnosis: Biliary atresia or genetic/metabolic liver diseases.

 

Treatment: Mainly supportive, including nutritional support and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation.

 

In acute cholecystitis (Option C): Filling of gallbladder is absent due to obstruction of cystic duct.

In Extrahepatic biliary atresia (EHBA) (Option A) and Bile duct stricture (Option D) there is absence of excretion of radioisotope into the intestines.

questions.solutionHtml:
>

Before 34 weeks of gestation with severe hypertension (BP > 160/110mm Hg), expectant management may prolong pregnancy to improve neonatal outcomes if maternal and fetal conditions are stable.

 

Algorithm for Treating Preeclampsia

Initial Evaluation
  • Perform comprehensive maternal and fetal evaluation.
  • CBC with platelet estimate, serum creatinine, LDH, AST, ALT, and proteinuria testing.
  • Fetal evaluation: USG for estimated fetal weight, amniotic fluid volume, and fetal antepartum testing.

Decision for Delivery vs Expectant Management
  • 34+ Weeks Gestation: Deliver promptly upon maternal stabilization or with labor/prelabor rupture of membranes; do not delay for steroid administration.
  • Before 34 Weeks Gestation with Severe Preeclampsia: Consider expectant management in a tertiary care setting if maternal and fetal conditions are stable.
  • 37+ Weeks Gestation with Gestational Hypertension or Preeclampsia Without Severe Features: Opt for delivery rather than expectant management upon diagnosis.
  • Before 37 Weeks Gestation with Gestational Hypertension or Preeclampsia Without Severe Features: Managed as an outpatient; requires frequent fetal and maternal evaluation. Deliver only if specific conditions necessitate immediate intervention.

Management During Expectant Management
  • Closely monitor maternal and fetal conditions.
  • Serial laboratory testing: CBC, liver enzymes, serum creatinine.
  • Use antihypertensive therapy for acute-onset severe hypertension (systolic ≥160 mm Hg or diastolic ≥110 mm Hg).
  • Administer antenatal corticosteroids and monitor for 48 hours if delivery is indicated before 34 weeks gestation. 

Regularly check for Conditions Necessitating Delivery Regardless of Gestational Age

Maternal Conditions

Fetal Conditions
  • HELLP syndrome
  • Pulmonary edema
  • Eclampsia
  • Suspected acute placental abruption, or vaginal bleeding without placenta previa
  • Uncontrolled severe-range blood pressure
  • Worsening renal function
  • Persistent headaches, epigastric/right upper quadrant pain
  • Visual disturbances
  • Motor deficits
  • Altered sensorium
  • Stroke
  • Myocardial infarction
  • Abnormal fetal testing
  • Fetal death
  • Fetus with low survival likelihood (lethal anomaly, Extreme prematurity)
  • Persistent reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery

Postpartum Management
  • Monitor blood pressure and symptoms post-delivery.
  • Consider NSAIDs for pain management instead of opioids.

 

Delivery is typically done at or after 34 weeks of gestation, not necessarily at 30 weeks without severe features (Option A ruled out).

 

Monitoring for fetal distress is part of ongoing management, not initial for severe preeclampsia without immediate delivery indications (Option C ruled out)

 

Corticosteroids are recommended if delivery is anticipated before 34 weeks also no need to terminate the pregnancy (Option D ruled out)

questions.solution: n> incontinence refers to a combination of two types of urinary incontinence: stress urinary incontinence (SUI) and urge urinary incontinence (UUI). This condition is characterised by symptoms of both types occurring concurrently in an individual. Individuals with mixed urinary incontinence experience symptoms of both SUI and UUI. They may have leakage of urine during activities that increase abdominal pressure (SUI), as well as sudden urges to urinate that lead to involuntary leakage (UUI). Types of urinary incontinence: Type Description Stress urinary incontinence Involuntary loss of urine with effort or physical exertion or when sneezing or coughing. Urgency urinary incontinence Involuntary loss of urine associated with urgency or sudden, compelling desire to void that is difficult to defer. Mixed urinary incontinence Involuntary loss of urine associated with urgency and with physical exertion, sneezing or coughing. Overactive bladder Urinary urgency, typically accompanied by frequency and nocturia, with or without urge urinary incontinence, in the absence of urinary tract infection or other obvious pathology. Nocturnal enuresis Involuntary loss of urine that occurs during sleep. Functional urinary incontinence Involuntary loss of urine that is due to cognitive, functional, or mobility impairments in the presence of an intact lower urinary tract system. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: b and Valdecoxib, selective COX-2 inhibitors, were withdrawn from the market due to their association with a higher risk of atherothrombotic events. COX-2 inhibitors reduce endothelial PGI2 production without affecting platelet TXA2 synthesis → Prothrombotic state → Increased cardiovascular risk. Hence, they should be reserved for high-risk peptic ulcer patients at the lowest dose and shortest duration and avoided in patients with a risk of heart disease. Aspirin and Naproxen (Options A and B): are safer for cardiovascular patients due to their antiplatelet effects. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet aggregation primarily by inhibiting COX-1, which reduces the risk of cardiovascular events. Similarly, Naproxen's longer half-life and COX inhibition contribute to cardiovascular safety. Nefopam (Option C): doesn't act on the COX enzyme. It is a serotonin-norepinephrine dopamine reuptake inhibitor (SNDRI). It is used to treat migraines and post-anesthetic shivering. questions.solution: y bleeding, pelvic pain, and a firm, irregularly enlarged uterus. Histopathology reveals interlacing bundles of smooth muscle cells with a characteristic whorled appearance. Fibroids have an Eosinophilic cytoplasm and oval nuclei (cigar-shaped) with blunt ends. Adenomyosis (Option A) is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, usually causing a uniformly enlarged and tender uterus. Histopathologically, adenomyosis shows endometrial glands and stroma interspersed within the myometrium. Endometrial Polyps (Option B) present with intermenstrual spotting rather than heavy bleeding. Histopathologically, endometrial polyps show irregularly shaped glands and a fibrous stroma, sometimes with blood vessels. Endometriosis (Option D) is endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus, causing chronic pain and infertility, with histopathology showing ectopic endometrial glands and stroma. @Neet_pg_bot

th:733px">

Ezetimibe

  • Disrupts cholesterol and phytosterol absorption in the small intestines via PCIL1 transporter protein interference.
  • Ezetimibe, with statins, enhances LDL-C reduction by inhibiting statin-induced cholesterol synthesis rise.

PCSK9 inhibitors

questions.stem: An infant was brought in due to concerns from her parents about her poor response to loud sounds and reduced reaction to environmental noises compared to her peers. The BERA test shows issues with wave V within the first 10 milliseconds. What site of pathology might this indicate?
questions.stemHtml: An infant was brought in due to concerns from her parents about her poor response to loud sounds and reduced reaction to environmental noises compared to her peers. The BERA test shows issues with wave V within the first 10 milliseconds. What site of pathology might this indicate?
questions.solution: ong>Explanation: The wave V in BERA (Brainstem evoked response audiometry) represents lateral lemniscus. BERA (brainstem-evoked response audiometry) also known as Auditory brainstem response (ABR) is a non-invasive technique to assess the auditory pathway from the cochlea through the 8th cranial nerve to the brain stem. Electrical potentials are generated in response to several click stimuli or tone bursts and picked up from the vertex by surface electrodes. It measures hearing sensitivity in the range of 1000-4000 Hz. In a normal person, 7 waves are produced in the first 10 ms indicating respective anatomical site as, Wave I Distal part of CN VIII Wave II Proximal part of CN VIII near the brainstem Wave III Cochlear nucleus (Option A) Wave IV Superior olivary complex (Option B) Wave V Lateral lemniscus (Option C) Wave VI and VII Inferior Colliculus (Option D) Uses of BERA: As a screening procedure for infants. To determine the threshold of hearing in infants (also in children and adults who do not cooperate) and in malingerers. To diagnose and differentiate retro cochlear pathology (acoustic neuroma) from cochlear. Best audiometric test for acoustic neuroma (delay in wave 5 is suggestive of acoustic neuroma). To diagnose brainstem pathology. To monitor CN VIII intraoperatively during surgery for acoustic neuromas. @Neet_pg_bot

MCHC measures the concentration of haemoglobin in red blood cells. In folate deficiency, MCHC is typically normal because the concentration of haemoglobin per cell is not affected; rather, it is the size of the cells (MCV) that is increased due to impaired maturation of red blood cells.

Laboratory Investigations in Folic Acid Deficiency

  • Increased homocysteine
  • Normal methylmalonate
  • Haemoglobin level consistently below 10 g% (Option D ruled out)
  • Stained blood film shows:
    • Hypersegmentation of neutrophils (5 or more lobes)
    • Macrocytosis and anisocytosis
    • Giant polymorphs
    • Megaloblasts
    • Howell-Jolly bodies (often in buffy coat preparations)
  • Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) > 100 µ³ (Option B ruled out)
  • Mean corpuscular haemoglobin (MCH) > 33 pg, but MCHC is normal
  • Associated with leukopenia and thrombocytopenia
  • Serum iron levels are normal or high; iron binding capacity is low
  • Red cell folate < 2 ng/mL (normal:2.8-8 ng/mL) (Option A ruled out)
  • Serum vitamin B12 < 90 pg/mL (normal: 300 pg/mL)
  • Serum bilirubin may be elevated
  • Bone marrow examination shows megaloblastic erythropoiesis

  • A ureterocele is a congenital dilation of the terminal part of the ureter where it enters the bladder. It consists of layers of ureteric and bladder epithelium.
  • Cobraneck appearance on IVU is a hallmark feature where a dilated contrast-filled ureter is surrounded by a thin rim of the ureteric wall and bladder mucosa, typically measuring less than 2 mm in diameter.

 

Ureterocele

 

 

 

 

Note: 

  • Maiden waist deformity is a term given to describe the medial deviation of both ureters. 
  • Commonly seen in retroperitoneal fibrosis or unilateral cases of retrocaval ureter.
  • The ureters take a narrow, waist-like shape, resembling the waist of a maiden, usually at the level of the lumbosacral junction.

Hydronephrosis (Option C): This condition results from obstruction, leading to dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces. However, it does not produce the specific cobra head appearance at the ureterovesical junction.

 

Renal calculi (Option D): While stones can cause flank pain and UTIs, they appear as radiopaque densities on imaging and do not have the cobra head sign seen with a ureterocele.

ght:1px solid #000000; border-top:1px solid #000000; vertical-align:top">

Histopathological Bodies in Microbiology

Leishman Donovan (LD) bodies

  • Found in untreated leishmaniasis (Kala Azar).
  • They are light blue, ellipsoid structures measuring 2-4 μm in length.
  • LD bodies have an eccentric nucleus and a smaller kinetosome at the opposite pole, the amastigote form.
  • These bodies are located within large macrophages (also known as Wright's cells).

Dohle bodies

  • Light blue-grey, oval, basophilic staining inclusions were found in the cytoplasm of neutrophils in the peripheral smear, representing dilated endoplasmic reticulum.
  • Seen in severe infections like sepsis.
  • Indicate defective neutrophil production and maturation.

Hendersen-Petersen bodies

  • Molluscum contagiosum, caused by a DNA virus, poxvirus, is characterised by the presence of large, ellipsoid intracytoplasmic inclusions in the stratum spinosum.
  • Present as umbilicated tan-coloured lesions on the skin, which on pressing, express a creamy material.
  • Stain - Phloxine tartrate.

Cowdry Type A bodies

  • Cowdry bodies are eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions made of nucleic acid and protein, seen in infections like herpes.
  • Type A (Lipschultz body)(found in herpes and yellow fever) appears as droplet-like masses with clear halos and chromatin margination around the nucleus.
  • Type B (associated with polio and adenovirus) lacks nuclear changes.

69277719652247cd559">pneumonia (PCP), now known as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, is a common opportunistic infection in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV/AIDS.

Pneumocystis jirovecii

Risk factors
  • HIV: CD4 < 200
  • Primary immunodeficiency states
  • Transplant recipients
  • Hematological malignancies

Clinical features

Transmitted by respiratory droplets and is asymptomatic in immunocompetent individuals. In immunocompromised patients, life-threatening pneumonia develops.

PCP - Pneumocystis Carinii pneumonia

  • Dyspnoea
  • Dry cough
  • Fever
  • Weight loss
  • B/L interstitial pneumonia

Diagnosis
  • HRCT: Bilateral ground-glass opacities (GGOs)
  • BAL: Gomori methenamine silver stain shows trophozoites with black-stained cyst walls, giving a “crushed ping-pong ball” appearance.

 

PCP in different subjects:

  1. Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia

    • A patient with pneumonia presenting with a dry cough and no sputum production is best investigated with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL).

    • Opportunistic fungal infection

    • Classically in HIV patients with CD4 <200

  2. Plasma cell pneumonia

    • BAL/biopsy shows lots of plasma cell.

  3. Ping-pong ball appearance

    • Cystic forms on Gomori methenamine silver stain → black, crushed ping-pong balls

  4. Pharmacology

    • P for Pneumocystis:

      • C for Cotrimoxazole → drug of choice

      • P for Pentamidine → used in severe cases

questions.solution: eta" data-dictid="979385c98a1692777192fb1721a16e">median incubation period is the time for 50% of cases to show symptoms after exposure. The incubation period is the time between infection and the first symptom appearance. During incubation, the pathogen multiplies until it reaches a threshold to cause symptoms. Most diseases aren't communicable during incubation, except for measles and chickenpox. Incubation periods vary by disease and individual, ranging from hours to years. Examples: Short (hours to days): Food poisoning, cholera. Medium (10 days to 3 weeks): Typhoid, COVID-19, measles. Long (weeks to years): Hepatitis, Rabies, leprosy. Non-infectious diseases like cancer also have incubation periods, often lasting months or years. Shortest time from exposure to symptom onset in 50% of cases (Option A) describes the minimum incubation period, not the median. Longest time from exposure to symptom onset in 50% of cases (Option B) describes the maximum incubation period, not the median. Average time from exposure to recovery in 50% of cases (Option C) describes the average recovery time, not the incubation period. @Neet_pg_bot

Measures the distance from the acromion to the lateral epicondyle with the arm in a neutral position. A lack of gap between the arm and the ruler indicates dislocation.

Type of Cyst

Description

Details

Functional Cyst

Fluid-filled sacs that form on the ovaries, typically during the menstrual cycle.

  •  2 Types:
    1. Follicular cysts form due to hormonal dysfunction prior to ovulation, leading to expansion of the follicular antrum with serous fluid.
    2. Corpus luteum cysts form due to excessive hemorrhage from the vascular corpus luteum following ovulation.
  • High-dose combination oral contraceptives (COCs) suppress ovarian activity and protect against cyst development.
  • Surgical excision is considered for large, persistent cysts or smaller ones causing persistent symptoms. Usually benign and not cancerous.

Gartner’s Cyst

Forms from remnants of the Wolffian duct

  • Located along vaginal walls
  • Can cause discomfort, urinary issues, or dyspareunia if large
  • Treatment may involve surgical removal if symptomatic

Skene’s Cyst

Located near the urethra in females, formed from the Skene’s glands.

  • Involved in lubrication of the urethral opening. Usually presents as a urethral diverticulum.
  • Cysts here can cause urinary problems, pain, or discomfort.
  • Treatment may include antibiotics for infection or surgical drainage/removal if necessary.

Nabothian Cyst

Mucus-filled cysts that occur on the cervix.

  • Form when mucus-producing glands in the cervix are covered by skin cells, trapping the mucus.
  • Generally harmless, asymptomatic and often found during routine pelvic exams.
  • No treatment is typically required unless they cause significant symptoms, in which case they can be drained or removed.

questions.solution: pacing="0" style="border-collapse:collapse; width:719px"> Mechanism of Action Effect on Smoking Cessation First-Line Drugs Bupropion (Option D) Blocks reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine in the brain Reduces nicotine withdrawal symptoms and cravings Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT) Provides controlled nicotine dose (patches, gum, lozenges, inhalers). Never given orally, sublingual due to its fast absorption Alleviates withdrawal symptoms and cravings, gradually reducing nicotine dependence Varenicline Binds to nicotine receptors in the brain, partially stimulating them. Most effective drug. Reduces cravings and pleasurable effects of smoking. Used in tobacco chewing. ding disorientation, dilated pupils, visual hallucinations (seeing vivid colors and patterns), tachycardia, and mild hypertension, are consistent with LSD intoxication.

Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD)

Chemical nature

Synthetic base derived from lysergic acid nucleus from ergot alkaloids

Common forms

Tablets, liquid, blotter paper ("blotter acid")

Potency

100 µg of LSD ≈ 10-15 mg of psilocybin ≈ 300-400 mg of mescaline

Onset and duration

Onset within an hour, peaks in 2-4 hours, lasts 8-12 hours

Common physiologic symptoms

• Dilated pupils

• Increased deep tendon motor reflexes

• Muscle tension

• Mild motor incoordination

• Ataxia

Occasional physiologic symptoms

• Increased heart rate

• Increased respiration

• Hypertension

• Nausea

• Decreased appetite

• Salivation

• Sweating

• Blurred vision

Psychological effects

• Visual and perceptual changes

• Altered sense of time

• Mood changes

• Possible anxiety or paranoia

• Possible feelings of insight or creativity

Associated phenomenon

• Flashback phenomenon

• Badtrip (also seen with cannabis)

• Reflex hallucination/ morbid synesthesia (may occur with other hallucinogens)

Tolerance

Develops quickly (2-3 days of repeated use), lost after 4-6 days of abstinence

Potential risks

• Accidents due to impaired judgment

• Rarely, a syndrome similar to neuroleptic malignant syndrome

• Possible triggering of anxiety or depression in some users

 

Date Rape Drugs:

Substances used to incapacitate victims, facilitating sexual assault by impairing memory and consciousness.

Common drugs include:

  1. Flunitrazepam (Rohypnol): A benzodiazepine causing deep sedation, muscle relaxation, and amnesia. Known for inducing memory loss, it is undetected due to its rapid action and dissociative effects.
  2. Gamma-Hydroxybutyric Acid (GHB): A CNS depressant causing euphoria, sedation, and amnesia. High doses lead to unconsciousness and respiratory depression. It is colorless and odorless, making it easy to mix into drinks.
  3. Gamma-Butyrolactone (GBL): A prodrug of GHB, converted in the body to produce similar sedative and amnesic effects.
  4. Ketamine: A dissociative anesthetic causing detachment, memory loss, and unconsciousness at higher doses.

While PCP can cause disorientation and altered perceptions, it typically presents with more severe symptoms such as aggressive behavior, nystagmus, and a more pronounced hypertension. The vivid visual hallucinations described are more characteristic of LSD (Option A)

Methamphetamine intoxication would typically present with more severe sympathomimetic effects, including significant hypertension, hyperthermia, and agitation. The visual hallucinations described are not typical of methamphetamine use (Option C)

While cannabis can cause anxiety and paranoia, the vivid visual hallucinations and dilated pupils are not typical. Cannabis-induced psychosis would more likely present with paranoid delusions rather than visual distortions (Option D)

Instruments used in Adenoid/ Tonsillectomy

Saint-Clair Thompson Adenoidectomy Curette with Cage

Purpose: Specialized instrument for adenoidectomy to remove adenoid tissue while minimizing trauma.

    • Curette inserted under the soft palate, tissue removed using an inferior to superior motion. (Option D ruled out)

Mollison's Tonsillar Dissector and Anterior Pillar Retractor

Purpose: Specialized instrument used in tonsillectomy procedures for enhanced visibility and separation of tonsil tissue.

    • Used to separate the tonsil from its surrounding capsule.
    • Facilitates the removal of the tonsil from the tonsillar bed.
  • Anterior Pillar Retraction:

    • Essential for examining the area for bleeding or remaining tissue post-removal.
  • Additional Uses:
    • Can retract the soft palate and uvula.
    • Aids in overall surgical access and visibility.

Eve's Tonsillar Snare

Purpose: Specialized instrument used in tonsillectomy to remove tonsils and minimize bleeding.

  • Crushing the Tonsil Pedicle:
    • Wire loop tightens around the tonsil's pedicle to crush it.
    • Reduces bleeding by compressing blood vessels.
  • Releasing Coagulation Factors:
    • Crushed tissue releases factors that accelerate coagulation.
    • Further aids in reducing bleeding.

logical umbilical hernia.

A physiological umbilical hernia is a normal developmental process where the intestines temporarily protrude into the base of the umbilical cord during early pregnancy. This occurs as the fetal abdomen is too small to accommodate the rapidly growing intestines. By around 12 weeks of gestation, the intestines typically return to the abdominal cavity, and the umbilical hernia resolves on its own. A follow-up ultrasound around 12 weeks is recommended to ensure proper closure and development.

 

Physiological Umbilical Hernia (PUH):

 

Occurs during early embryogenesis due to rapid growth of the midgut and liver, temporarily exceeding the size of the abdominal cavity.

 

  • Midgut Herniation (6th Week): The midgut herniates into the umbilical cord as the abdominal cavity is too small. It undergoes a 90-degree counterclockwise rotation around the superior mesenteric artery.
  • Midgut Retraction (10th-12th Week): The abdominal cavity expands, allowing the midgut to return. During retraction, an additional 180-degree counterclockwise rotation completes the 270-degree total, positioning the intestines.

 

Failure to Regress: Omphalocele: If the midgut doesn't return, omphalocele occurs, where organs remain herniated through the umbilical ring, covered by a membrane. It differs from Gastroschisis, where the organs protrude without a membrane.

questions.stemHtml: A 1-day-old newborn presents with respiratory distress. A chest X-ray is performed and is given below. Based on the findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: 927771899480554f5a">Hernia (Bochdalek type) Explanation: The given chest x-ray shows loops of bowel in the right thoracic cavity, mediastinal shift to the left, and decreased right lung aeration, which is consistent with Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia. Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH): CDH is the intrathoracic herniation of abdominal contents due to congenital defects in the diaphragm. Types of CDH : Bochdalek Hernia : Occurs through the posterolateral pleuroperitoneal canal, most commonly on the left side . Morgagni Hernia : Anterior hernia located at the right cardiophrenic angle. Fig. Schematic representation of CDH Radiologic Features : Chest Radiograph (CXR): Bochdalek hernia: Dome-shaped soft tissue opacity in the posterolateral thorax, often left-sided . May show gas-filled bowel loops or fat content in the thoracic cavity. Mediastinal shift away from the herniation due to mass effect. On the lateral view , hernias appear above the posterior costophrenic recess . CT/MRI : Visualizes herniation of fat, bowel, spleen, or kidney through a diaphragmatic defect. Important for distinguishing from other masses like cystic adenomatoid malformation or pericardial cyst . CT provides clearer differentiation of soft-tissue or fatty mass protruding through the diaphragm. Complications : Associated with hypoplasia of the ipsilateral lung , leading to respiratory distress, especially in neonates. Neonates may present with respiratory distress and mediastinal deviation. Esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula (Option B) : The primary abnormality may show air in the esophagus or stomach (if a fistula is present) and sometimes an absence of gas in the abdomen if there is no fistula. This condition doesn't present with bowel loops in the thorax or a large diaphragmatic defect. Pulmonary sequestration (Option C): It presents as a mass in the lower lobe of the lung, often with an abnormal vascular supply seen on advanced imaging like CT angiography. No bowel loops or significant mediastinal shift would be seen. Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) (Option D) appears as cystic masses within the lung, but the cysts are within the lung parenchyma, not abdominal contents in the thorax. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
927771899480554f5a">Hernia (Bochdalek type)

Explanation:

The given chest x-ray shows loops of bowel in the right thoracic cavity, mediastinal shift to the left, and decreased right lung aeration, which is consistent with Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia.

Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH):

  1. CDH is the intrathoracic herniation of abdominal contents due to congenital defects in the diaphragm.
  2. Types of CDH:
    • Bochdalek Hernia: Occurs through the posterolateral pleuroperitoneal canal, most commonly on the left side.
    • Morgagni Hernia: Anterior hernia located at the right cardiophrenic angle.

Fig. Schematic representation of CDH

  1. Radiologic Features:
    • Chest Radiograph (CXR):
      • Bochdalek hernia: Dome-shaped soft tissue opacity in the posterolateral thorax, often left-sided.
      • May show gas-filled bowel loops or fat content in the thoracic cavity.
      • Mediastinal shift away from the herniation due to mass effect.
      • On the lateral view, hernias appear above the posterior costophrenic recess.
    • CT/MRI:
      • Visualizes herniation of fat, bowel, spleen, or kidney through a diaphragmatic defect.
      • Important for distinguishing from other masses like cystic adenomatoid malformation or pericardial cyst.
      • CT provides clearer differentiation of soft-tissue or fatty mass protruding through the diaphragm.
  2. Complications:
    • Associated with hypoplasia of the ipsilateral lung, leading to respiratory distress, especially in neonates.
    • Neonates may present with respiratory distress and mediastinal deviation.

 

Esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula (Option B):

  • The primary abnormality may show air in the esophagus or stomach (if a fistula is present) and sometimes an absence of gas in the abdomen if there is no fistula.
  • This condition doesn't present with bowel loops in the thorax or a large diaphragmatic defect.

 

Pulmonary sequestration (Option C):

  • It presents as a mass in the lower lobe of the lung, often with an abnormal vascular supply seen on advanced imaging like CT angiography.
  • No bowel loops or significant mediastinal shift would be seen.

 

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) (Option D) appears as cystic masses within the lung, but the cysts are within the lung parenchyma, not abdominal contents in the thorax.

questions.solution: 77718566066add68">cyanosis at birth, pansystolic murmur due to tricuspid regurgitation, mother’s history of Bipolar (Lithium exposed pregnancy), and the characteristic Himalayan P wave on ECG is most consistent with Atrialization of the right ventricle. This condition is also known as Ebstein's Anomaly. Ebstein's Anomaly: Associated with Lithium exposure during pregnancy. Pathophysiology: Downward displacement/prolapse of the tricuspid valve. Part of the right ventricular volume becomes part of the right atrium (atrialization of the right ventricle). Consequences: Tricuspid Regurgitation: Prolapsed valve → Blood from the right ventricle regurgitates into the right atrium. RVOT (Right Ventricular Outflow Tract) Obstruction: Prolapsed valve partly occludes blood flow towards the pulmonary artery → Cyanosis. Features: Cyanosis at birth or during the neonatal period. Pansystolic murmur: Due to tricuspid regurgitation. Quadruple Rhythm: Irregular blood flow in the right heart, RVOT obstruction, and tricuspid regurgitation → Multiple added sounds and ejection clicks. X-Ray Findings: Right atrial enlargement due to regurgitation from the right ventricle and atrialization of the right ventricle. RA forms the right heart border, which displaces laterally and appears on X-ray as a box-shaped heart. ECG: Himalayan P Waves Tetralogy of Fallot (Option A): Characterized by cyanosis, a systolic ejection murmur, and right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. X-ray typically shows a boot-shaped heart. Transposition of the Great Arteries (Option C): Presents with severe cyanosis, often with a systolic murmur if there is associated outflow obstruction. X-ray findings usually show an "egg-on-a-string" appearance. Ventricular Septal Defect (Option D): Presents with a pansystolic murmur and may cause pulmonary overcirculation, but the X-ray findings would generally show an enlarged heart with increased pulmonary markings. @Neet_pg_bot

  • This condition is also known as Ebstein's Anomaly.

Ebstein's Anomaly:

  • Associated with Lithium exposure during pregnancy.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Downward displacement/prolapse of the tricuspid valve.
    • Part of the right ventricular volume becomes part of the right atrium (atrialization of the right ventricle).
  • Consequences:
    • Tricuspid Regurgitation: Prolapsed valve → Blood from the right ventricle regurgitates into the right atrium.
    • RVOT (Right Ventricular Outflow Tract) Obstruction: Prolapsed valve partly occludes blood flow towards the pulmonary artery → Cyanosis.
  • Features:
    • Cyanosis at birth or during the neonatal period.
    • Pansystolic murmur: Due to tricuspid regurgitation.
    • Quadruple Rhythm: Irregular blood flow in the right heart, RVOT obstruction, and tricuspid regurgitation → Multiple added sounds and ejection clicks.
  • X-Ray Findings:
    • Right atrial enlargement due to regurgitation from the right ventricle and atrialization of the right ventricle.
    • RA forms the right heart border, which displaces laterally and appears on X-ray as a box-shaped heart.

  • ECG: Himalayan P Waves

 

Tetralogy of Fallot (Option A):

  • Characterized by cyanosis, a systolic ejection murmur, and right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. X-ray typically shows a boot-shaped heart.

Transposition of the Great Arteries (Option C):

  • Presents with severe cyanosis, often with a systolic murmur if there is associated outflow obstruction.
  • X-ray findings usually show an "egg-on-a-string" appearance.

Ventricular Septal Defect (Option D):

  • Presents with a pansystolic murmur and may cause pulmonary overcirculation, but the X-ray findings would generally show an enlarged heart with increased pulmonary markings.

questions.solution: n: The patient's symptoms and the histopathological findings of hemosiderin - laden macrophages known as ‘ Heart failure cells ’ are consistent with Left-sided heart failure. This condition is characterized by the heart's inability to pump blood effectively, causing backflow of blood, leading to pulmonary congestion and oedema. In pulmonary edema, the lungs appear wet and boggy, and chest X-ray shows characteristic Kerley B lines. Chronic congestion and microhemorrhages in the lungs result in the accumulation of hemosiderin - laden macrophages (Heart failure cells). These cells can be identified using special stains such as Perl's or Prussian blue , which detect hemosiderin's presence. @Neet_pg_bot

Scarlet Fever

Group A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis is associated with a characteristic rash caused due to a pyrogenic exotoxin (erythrogenic toxin) produced by GAS in individuals lacking antitoxin antibodies.

Caused By

Group A Streptococcus (GAS)

Incidence and Virulence

Less common and less virulent now compared to the past, with incidence depending on toxin strains and the population's immunity.

Clinical Features
  • Rash appears within 24-48 hours, starting around the neck and spreading to the trunk and extremities.
  • Rash is a diffuse, finely papular, erythematous eruption causing bright-red discoloration, which blanches on pressure.
  • Rash is accentuated in the creases of the elbow, axilla, and groin (Pastia lines) and gives the skin a goose-pimple appearance.

  • After 3-4 days, the rash fades, followed by desquamation starting on the face and progressing downward.
  • Desquamation may occur around fingernails, palms, and soles.
  • Tongue is coated with swollen papillae, which later give a "strawberry tongue" appearance after desquamation.
  • Pharyngitis.

Diagnosis
  • Classic scarlet fever is typically straightforward to diagnose.
  • A history of recent exposure to GAS is helpful.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying GAS in the pharynx.

Treatment

  • Antibiotic therapy should be started immediately.
  • Drug of choice: Penicillin or amoxicillin for 10 days.
  • Alternative for Penicillin Allergy: Oral cephalosporins, clindamycin, Macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin) for 10 days or azalide (azithromycin) for 5 days.
  • Injection: Benzathine penicillin G single dose intramuscular injection for those unlikely to complete oral therapy.

Complication

    • Peritonsillar abscess

    • Mastoiditis
    • Sinusitis
    • Group A Streptococcus (GAS) pneumonia

The Ujjawala scheme

The Ujjawala scheme, launched in India on December 4, 2007, by the Ministry of Women and Child Development, is a comprehensive program to combat trafficking. The scheme is primarily implemented through NGOs.

Objectives/Goals

Strategies to Achieve Goals

Prevention

  • Formation of community vigilance and adolescent groups, awareness creation
  • preparation of IEC (Information, Education, Communication) material, organization of workshops.

Rescue

  • Safe withdrawal of victims from the place of exploitation.

Rehabilitation

  • Providing safe shelter, basic amenities, medical care, legal aid, vocational training, and employment opportunities to victims.

Reintegration

  • Supporting victims in their reintegration into society.

Repatriation

  • Providing support to cross-border victims for their safe return to their home countries.

 

The Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY) (Option B) is a key initiative to provide rural and underprivileged households with access to clean cooking fuels like LPG, replacing traditional cooking fuels. It comes under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas (MOPNG)

The UJALA (Unnat Jyoti by Affordable LEDs for All) scheme (Option C) aims to promote energy efficiency by distributing LED bulbs at affordable prices. This initiative reduces energy consumption and lowers household electricity bills. It also contributes to environmental sustainability by cutting down carbon emissions. The Ministry of Power administers it.

The PM Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana (PM Saubhagya scheme) (Option D) was initiated in September 2017 to provide electricity to every household by December 2018. The Ministry of Power administers it.

questions.solutionHtml:
Prevertebral abscess, which is formed as a complication of cervical spine caries due to TB, presents as a fluctuant swelling in the posterior pharyngeal wall centrally.

 

Prevertebral Abscess:

Prevertebral space
  • Extent: Base of skull to coccyx
  • Location: Between vertebrae on one side and prevertebral muscles and the prevertebral fascia on the other

Aetiology
  • Tubercular in nature, caused by:
    • Caries of the cervical spine (central abscess behind prevertebral fascia)
    • Tuberculous infection of retropharyngeal lymph nodes (unilateral abscess behind buccopharyngeal fascia)

Clinical Features
  • Throat discomfort
  • Mild dysphagia
  • Fluctuant swelling in posterior pharyngeal wall, either centrally or on one side of midline

Treatment
  • Incision and drainage
  • Antitubercular therapy

 

Comparison between retropharyngeal and prevertebral abscesses:

 

Retropharyngeal (Option B)

Prevertebral (Option A)

Location of the space

Behind the pharynx, between the buccopharyngeal fascia and prevertebral fascia, extending from the base of the skull to the bifurcation of the trachea.

Between vertebrae on one side and prevertebral muscles and the prevertebral fascia on the other, extenting from the base of skull to coccyx

Etiology

  • Children under 3 years (common)-suppuration of retropharyngeal lymph nodes
  • Adults-penetrating injuries to the posterior pharyngeal wall or cervical esophagus.

Tubercular in nature, caused by: Caries of the cervical spine or tuberculous infection of retropharyngeal lymph nodes

Clinical features

  • Dysphagia
  • Breathing difficulty
  • Stridor
  • Croupy cough
  • Torticollis
  • Unilateral bulge in the posterior pharyngeal wall
  • Throat discomfort
  • Mild dysphagia
  • Fluctuant swelling in posterior pharyngeal wall, either centrally or on one side of midline

 

 

Parapharyngeal abscess (Option C): Incorrect as it causes lateral wall bulge, trismus, and more severe systemic symptoms.

Peritonsillar abscess (Option D): Incorrect since it is peritonsillar, not posterior pharyngeal, and presents with uvular deviation.

  • Long, almost straight blades

  • Asymmetrical blades (one solid, one fenestrated)
  • Specifically for the after-coming head in breech deliveries.
  • Allows application when access to the fetal head is limited.

The Triad of retinitis pigmentosa:

  • Waxy disc pallor
  • Attenuated arteries

Retinitis pigmentosa: 

  • Inheritance: Most commonly sporadic, but AD, AR, X-linked are all possible.
  • Most common systemic association: Usher’s syndrome (RP + deafness).
  • Treatment: No definitive cure. Trials with docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) showed possible slowing of progression.

 

 

Chronic Central Serous Chorioretinopathy (Option B): Typically shows a serous detachment at the macula with a ring reflex.

Age-Related Macular Degeneration (Option C): Presents with drusen (dry) or choroidal neovascular membranes (wet) at the macula.

Toxoplasmic Retinochoroiditis (Option D): Characterized by the classic “headlight in the fog” appearance.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old female with hypertension and heart failure is prescribed an ACE inhibitor for blood pressure control. What is the most significant drug interaction to be cautious about when prescribing ACE inhibitors?
questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old female with hypertension and heart failure is prescribed an ACE inhibitor for blood pressure control. What is the most significant drug interaction to be cautious about when prescribing ACE inhibitors?
questions.solution: can pose significant risks, especially the interaction with potassium-sparing diuretics. Here are some key interactions and their clinical implications: Drug Interaction Mechanism Clinical Implication ACE Inhibitors + Potassium Supplements/K-sparing diuretics Risk of hyperkalemia due to reduced aldosterone secretion by ACE inhibitors combined with potassium-retaining agents. Monitoring serum potassium levels is crucial to avoid hyperkalemia, which can cause serious cardiac issues such as arrhythmias. ACE Inhibitors + NSAIDs NSAIDs can reduce the anti-hypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors and decrease renal blood flow, increasing the risk of acute renal failure (ARF) or oliguria. Use caution when combining NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors, and closely monitor renal function, particularly in high-risk patients. ACE Inhibitors + Lithium ACE inhibitors can increase the reabsorption of lithium, potentially leading to lithium toxicity. Monitor lithium levels carefully when starting or adjusting ACE inhibitors in patients taking lithium, and adjust the lithium dosage as needed. ACE Inhibitors + Antacids Reduced bioavailability of ACE inhibitors due to binding with antacids. Administer ACE inhibitors at least two hours before or after antacids to maintain their efficacy. ACE Inhibitors + Diuretics Diuretics enhance the hypotensive effects of ACE inhibitors by depleting sodium and raising renin levels. In patients already on diuretics, start ACE inhibitors at a low dose to minimise the risk of excessive blood pressure reduction initially. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
can pose significant risks, especially the interaction with potassium-sparing diuretics. Here are some key interactions and their clinical implications:

Drug Interaction

Mechanism

Clinical Implication

ACE Inhibitors + Potassium Supplements/K-sparing diuretics

Risk of hyperkalemia due to reduced aldosterone secretion by ACE inhibitors combined with potassium-retaining agents.

Monitoring serum potassium levels is crucial to avoid hyperkalemia, which can cause serious cardiac issues such as arrhythmias.

ACE Inhibitors + NSAIDs

NSAIDs can reduce the anti-hypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors and decrease renal blood flow, increasing the risk of acute renal failure (ARF) or oliguria.

Use caution when combining NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors, and closely monitor renal function, particularly in high-risk patients.

ACE Inhibitors + Lithium

ACE inhibitors can increase the reabsorption of lithium, potentially leading to lithium toxicity.

Monitor lithium levels carefully when starting or adjusting ACE inhibitors in patients taking lithium, and adjust the lithium dosage as needed.

ACE Inhibitors + Antacids

Reduced bioavailability of ACE inhibitors due to binding with antacids.

Administer ACE inhibitors at least two hours before or after antacids to maintain their efficacy.

ACE Inhibitors + Diuretics

Diuretics enhance the hypotensive effects of ACE inhibitors by depleting sodium and raising renin levels.

In patients already on diuretics, start ACE inhibitors at a low dose to minimise the risk of excessive blood pressure reduction initially.
